title_en: Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade postponed, as New York braces for huge storm
content_en:
The unprecedented move comes amid concerns about how the event’s massive balloons would fare during the intense winds predicted.
A Buzz Lightyear balloon rests under protective netting during the inflation on Wednesday for Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade in New York. Photo: AFP
Macy’s 100th Thanksgiving Day Parade will also be a first: organisers made an unprecedented decision to postpone the event to Saturday because of bad weather.
The annual parade, originally scheduled for Thursday, has been moved “out of an abundance of caution” and following consultation with city officials about the severe weather, Macy’s said in a statement on Wednesday.
“Our team is now working through the complex operational logistics required to bring the Parade to life on Saturday, and we will share additional details as they are finalised,” the company said.
The postponement came as New York is set to get slammed by a storm bringing intense winds and rain to the region, which had raised worries about how the parade’s massive balloons would fare while floating through the windswept canyons between Manhattan’s skyscrapers and over throngs of spectators lining the streets below.
The National Weather Service has issued a high wind warning and a coastal flood warning for Thursday into Friday.
Workers inflate a Spider-Man balloon on Wednesday for the 100th Annual Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade in New York. Photo: EPA
The city’s emergency management agency has been warning residents about the possible storm, with officials banning empty articulated lorries from bridges on Thursday morning because of the wind.
NBC, which airs the parade, said it will instead broadcast a rerun of the 2025 edition Thursday. It was not immediately clear whether the event’s expansive line-up of performers would also shift to the new date.
The parade’s iconic balloons were well on the way to being inflated when the postponement was announced. Macy’s representatives had repeatedly put off interviews on-site, raising eyebrows among the city’s news media ahead of the official postponement.
A spokesman for the retail giant said it was the first time the event has been postponed. It was cancelled for three years – in 1942, 1943 and 1944 – during World War II, the spokesman said.
Workers inflate a Donkey balloon on Wednesday before the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade in New York. Photo: EPA
The city has long had measures in place that dictate whether to lower the balloons or cancel their flights entirely if the wind gets too strong, due to concerns that strong winds can knock them off course and into spectators along the parade route.
The rules were put in place after high winds sent a balloon careering into a metal pole during the 1997 parade, leaving a woman in a coma.
Bad weather in the past has caused balloons to be flown a bit lower than usual, with each inflatable character having a distinct risk profile that includes its size and weight and optimal altitudes for differing wind speeds.
The rescheduled parade will kick off at 8.30am on Saturday, Macy’s said in a statement.
By Associated Press

title_en: US trading partners’ patience wears thin as Trump slaps on new tariffs
content_en:
Resignation and frustration reign as predictable US president announces fresh tariffs on 14 major economies, including China.
US President Donald Trump announces worldwide tariffs on April 2, 2025. Photo: Getty Images/TNS
Major US trading partners and companies on the economic front lines decried US President Donald Trump’s latest tariff salvo on Wednesday, even as they expressed resignation, as his playbook has become more predictable and better telegraphed with repeated use.
This followed the White House’s proposal of fresh tariffs a few hours earlier on 14 major economies, including China, a week after Trump met Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen.
The new levies, subject to a public comment period, would lift total duties on targeted economies from 15 to 20 per cent. This comes as the transactional US president looks for alternatives after the US Supreme Court struck down his broad-based “emergency” tariffs in February.
“Partners have been waiting for this shoe to drop for some time,” said Wendy Cutler, senior vice-president with the Asia Society Policy Institute. “Many have publicly and privately pushed back in recent months, stressing that they are being wrongly accused of producing too much in selected sectors.”
The latest tariff announcement tied to excess industrial capacity follows other levies outlined in July tied to forced labour.
[embedded media]
This steady drumbeat of trade barriers will only increase incentives among economies worldwide to shift their supply chains away from US shores. “Make no mistake. These tariffs will continue to accelerate diversification efforts,” added Cutler, a former senior US trade negotiator.
Trading partners from Beijing to Brussels expressed their displeasure on Wednesday even as they pushed back on the overproduction rationale.
“Tariff wars and trade wars serve no one’s interests,” said Chinese foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun. “The so-called issue of overcapacity is a false proposition, and China opposes using it as a pretext for political manipulation.”
“India does not have structural excess capacity in any sector,” the country’s Ministry of Commerce and Industry said, while Bernd Lange, head of the European Union Parliament’s trade committee, called such charges “absurd”.
“If Washington breaches its commitments, the EU must act swiftly,” Lange added. “It has the legal means to do so.”
South Korea, like many countries, said it was studying Wednesday’s US Trade Representative announcement, adding in a statement that an ultimate rate of 15 per cent would be a “good outcome”, while noting that Washington has left open the possibility of raising it to 25 per cent “depending on the outcome of future consultations”.
The tone from many countries after the announcement was relatively muted, however, analysts said. The Supreme Court slapdown of his use of the International Emergency Economic Powers Act has blunted his ability to apply punitive trade measures at will, they said.
And under the various workarounds the self-declared “tariff man” has reached for since then, including Section 301, 232, 122 and 338 trade provisions, most involve lead time, laid-out processes and hearings that reduce the impact and make planning easier.
This stands in sharp contrast to the global shock when his 2025 “Liberation Day” onslaught was announced.
US small business owners unhappy with latest tariff proposal
That does not mean, however, that small business owners welcome his latest move, as they cited its impact on input costs and prices for consumers already grappling with a US affordability crisis.
“Customers can’t afford more price increases, but small businesses can’t afford to absorb tariffs on top [of] tariffs either,” said Dan Anthony, executive director of “We Pay the Tariffs”, a coalition of small businesses.
“As if their unpopularity wasn’t bad enough, the tariffs also have failed to achieve any of the administration’s stated objectives,” he added.
Experts widely viewed elevated tariffs, combined with higher energy prices triggered by the conflict in Iran, as key drivers of Republican setbacks in the recent US midterm elections – a political cost that has done little to deter the White House from pressing ahead with fresh import duties.
[embedded media]
“Any additional tariffs will further exacerbate the situation and put many restaurants in the USA on the precipice of failure,” said Fred Mortati, the owner of Orlando Food Sales, a New Jersey-based food importer and distributor.
“We are begging Congress to listen to its constituents and not allow further price increases by way of additional tariffs.”
Figures released on Wednesday showed the Personal Consumption Expenditures price index increased 0.3 per cent in October from a month earlier, lifting the annual inflation rate to 3.8 per cent.
Democrats’ growing clout after Trump’s party was drubbed in the midterms has also led to more pushback.
Chuck Schumer, the Senate Democratic leader, said Wednesday that the president’s actions continue to alienate allies while “passing the costs onto American families”.
“Donald Trump never learns,” he wrote on social media, adding that the “bad actor is China” even as the administration has failed to address the role of the Asian giant.
“Change is coming in January,” Schumer promised.
The Congressional Asian Pacific American Caucus (CAPAC) also said Trump’s “reckless trade wars” have made life costlier for Asian-American, Native Hawaiians and Pacific Islanders, as many of them rely on imports that cannot be produced domestically.
The caucus vowed to use the incoming Democratic majority to roll back the duties.
“Next year, CAPAC members will reclaim Congress’s constitutional authority under Article I to regulate trade and work to end these costly tariffs once and for all,” said Representative Grace Meng, the New York Democrat who chairs the caucus.
[embedded media]
Congress has the power under the Constitution to levy taxes and tariffs and to regulate foreign commerce, authority that lawmakers have largely delegated to the executive branch over the decades.
But analysts said China has concluded that it is competitive enough to weather 20 per cent tariffs, especially if other countries face similar US restrictions, and will continue to back the trade truce despite Trump’s weakened political stature.
“Beijing will prioritise stability over exploiting Trump’s weakened position, responding proportionately to US restrictions, while mutual vulnerabilities will deter severe escalation,” said Dominic Chiu, senior analyst with the Eurasia Group, in a report.
A September study by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York found that for every percentage point increase in average tariffs, consumer goods prices rose by about a quarter of a per cent after one year.
Analysis shows 90 per cent of 2025 tariffs paid by US producers, consumers
The analysis also showed that nearly 90 per cent of the 2025 tariffs were paid by US producers and consumers, not the export country, as Trump has claimed.
While the new tariffs are unlikely to directly disrupt the fragile US-China truce, the move adds another layer of complexity to ongoing negotiations over extending the Busan agreement, which expires on January 10, 2027.
Under the deal signed in South Korea last year, Washington reduced tariffs on certain Chinese imports and suspended additional trade restrictions in return for a pause on China’s rare earth export controls and a pledge to resume US agricultural purchases.
Analysts said the timing of Wednesday’s tariff announcement – after the politically sensitive midterm elections and last week’s Trump-Xi meeting and three weeks before the G20 convenes in Miami – was hardly coincidental.
And it lets Trump keep much of what he relishes: leverage to make deals, to counter others’ leverage and to impose his will on smaller players.
“Of note, the US indicated that it retains the flexibility to raise these tariffs if ongoing bilateral talks fail or China does not live up to its commitments,” said Cutler.
“Clearly, the US is using these tariffs as leverage to secure expected shipments of critical minerals and rare earths, and further purchases of US agricultural goods.”
China on Tuesday extended its suspension of export restrictions on US-bound shipments of gallium, germanium and antimony until January 27, aligning the two-month reprieve with ongoing talks over extending the Busan agreement.
Both sides are also taking steps to implement the US-China Board of Trade, which oversees tariff-reduced trade in non-sensitive goods worth up to US$30 billion on each side.

title_en: US federal court blocks new Trump birthright citizenship executive order
content_en:
US judge on Wednesday blocked enforcement of US president’s second executive order after US Supreme Court rejected ‌his initial effort.
A protester holds a sign in support of birthright citizenship outside the US Supreme Court in Washington, in May 2025. Photo: AP
A federal judge on Wednesday blocked US President Donald Trump’s latest executive order aimed at restricting birthright citizenship, dealing another setback to his ongoing effort to redefine what it means to be born an American.
“Enough is enough,” said Cody Wofsy, deputy director of the American Civil Liberties Union’s Immigrants’ Rights Project. “The Supreme Court has twice rejected efforts to gut birthright citizenship, in 1898 and again earlier this year.
“Third time is not the charm, and the president needs to accept that birthright citizenship is the law of the land.”
Limiting birthright citizenship has been a cornerstone of Trump’s second-term agenda as part of his aggressive immigration agenda, and he has sought to curtail it in multiple ways since returning to office, including in a previous executive order the US Supreme Court struck down earlier this year.
Trump signed the initial executive order on his first day back in office in 2025.
US President Donald Trump signs an executive order on birthright citizenship in the Oval Office in January 2025. Photo: AP
That order directed federal agencies not to recognise the citizenship of children born in the US to parents who were undocumented or present on temporary visas.
The Supreme Court ruled 6-3 against him in Trump vs Barbara in June, holding that children born in the US to parents who are unlawfully or temporarily present are citizens at birth under the 14th Amendment.
Following his Supreme Court loss, Trump issued another executive order in August that sought to expand the categories of children who the government says are not entitled to birthright citizenship.
Among those targeted were children whose parents worked for foreign governments or certain international organisations, as well as children born through commercial birth tourism and surrogacy arrangements.
In response, the American Civil Liberties Union and other advocacy groups filed a lawsuit, Nathan vs Trump, in September on behalf of those who would be subject to the new executive order, leading to Wednesday’s preliminary decision.
In his preliminary injunction on the second executive order on Wednesday, US District Judge Christopher Cooper in Washington said that “Barbara’s ink had scarcely dried when the President issued a second executive order”.
Cooper noted that the Supreme Court had already recognised that these children are US citizens.
“As the Supreme Court has made clear, however, the president cannot carve out new exceptions to birthright citizenship for children born within the United States and subject to its laws,” wrote Cooper.
The judge also highlighted that the practice of birth tourism violates US law, “under which ‘obtaining US citizenship for a child’ is an impermissible basis for a tourist visa”.
Trump has often taken advantage of the courts’ slow pace to impose “facts on the ground”, even if there is a high likelihood his administration’s actions will be overruled.
In the months since the Supreme Court ruling, the Trump administration has increasingly focused on birth tourism, particularly cases involving Chinese nationals.
“I would like to congratulate President Xi and the Great Country of China on their massive Birthright Citizenship WIN! President DONALD J. TRUMP,” Trump wrote on social media after the Supreme Court verdict.
While birth tourism exists, available statistics indicate the practice is very rare.
Cooper is not the only judge to block the second executive order.
In September, US District Judge Deborah Boardman in Maryland issued a preliminary injunction at the request of immigrant rights advocates, noting that the president’s order was “almost certainly unconstitutional”.
By Lucy Quaggin

title_en: Colombia quiet as China says lawmakers’ Taiwan trip crossed its ‘first red line’
content_en:
Beijing’s embassy objects after senator dubbed Taipei’s envoy ‘ambassador’, but De la Espriella’s ministry does not comment on controversy.
Taiwanese Foreign Minister Lin Chia-lung met with Colombian Senator Luis Perez in Taipei in September 2025 to strengthen bilateral cooperation and economic ties. Photo: CNA
A multiparty group of Colombian lawmakers visiting Taiwan has drawn a formal protest from China, while President Abelardo de la Espriella’s government has stayed silent for two days as of Wednesday, even as the pressure from Beijing has intensified.
China’s embassy in Bogota demanded on Monday that both the government and Congress “publicly reiterate” their commitment to the one-China principle and “immediately take effective measures to correct the error and eliminate the negative impact”.
It called Taiwan the “first insurmountable red line” in relations with Colombia, which switched diplomatic recognition from Taipei to Beijing in 1980.
Beijing’s sharpest complaint concerned the way one lawmaker addressed the head of the Taipei Commercial Office in Bogota, Taiwan’s unofficial mission in Colombia.
Senator German Rodriguez of the right-wing Salvacion Nacional movement called him “ambassador” in a video recorded before the trip and listed Taiwan among Colombia’s friendly “countries”, according to Colombian media.
[embedded media]
The embassy said the office was “merely an unofficial economic and trade body without any diplomatic status” and that the lawmakers had travelled “in an official capacity” despite “solemn representations and repeated dissuasion” from Beijing.
It also asked Bogota to halt all official exchanges with the Taiwanese authorities and accused Taipei of winning over foreign politicians “through money and deception”.
The Taipei office answered on social media that it rejected “claims that do not correspond to reality” and that Beijing had offered “no concrete evidence”.
Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-governed island by force and is committed by law to supplying it with weapons.
The nine senators and representatives landed in Taipei on Monday and are due to leave on Friday. They belong to seven parties, from former president Gustavo Petro’s leftist Pacto Historico party to right-wing allies of the government, and all sit on the congressional committees for foreign affairs and trade.
As of Wednesday afternoon, neither De la Espriella nor Foreign Minister Omar Bula had said anything about the protest.
China is Colombia’s second-largest trading partner after the United States. When its top legislator Zhao Leji hosted lower house speaker Nicolas Barguil and a multiparty delegation in Beijing earlier this month, Barguil told him that Colombia “firmly supports” the one-China principle, according to Xinhua.
Third congressional trip to Taipei in 14 months
Colombian lawmakers have travelled to Taipei three times since September 2025, when a Taiwan friendship caucus led by Senator Jose Luis Perez met Taiwanese Foreign Minister Lin Chia-lung.
Two months later, the chairs of the Senate and lower house foreign affairs committees told Lin they would push for Colombia to reopen an office on the island.

title_en: Massive blaze kills at least 30 in Cairo, Egypt, after fuel truck overturns
content_en:
39 ambulances were sent to the scene after a fire erupted in a densely populated section of the capital.
Damaged cars are seen as firefighters extinguish a fire involving a vehicle carrying petroleum products just outside Cairo, Egypt, on Wednesday. Photo: AP
A fire erupted in Egypt’s capital on Wednesday, killing at least 30 people, according to the health ministry, after a fuel truck reportedly overturned on a packed highway.
Footage shot by passers-by showed a massive blaze and huge clouds of smoke rising from the site in Cairo’s densely populated Al-Waraq neighbourhood in Imbaba district.
State media reported that the fire broke out when a truck loaded with fuel overturned on a crowded highway.
The health ministry said 39 ambulances were sent to the scene, and 15 people were taken to hospital with injuries.
Images from the site showed a grisly aftermath, with cars burnt out from the blaze apparently caused by the fuel truck overturning, as firefighters doused the truck’s wreckage.
Flames are seen in the Al-Waraq neighbourhood of Imbaba district in Cairo, Egypt, on Wednesday. Photo: UGC via AFP
A crowd and emergency services gathered at the scene as a bulldozer removed a car’s burnt-out wreckage, images showed.
Egypt, with its informal residential areas and often dilapidated infrastructure, has suffered several deadly fires in recent years.
Slow response times of emergency services are not unusual in the country, where neighbourhood residents routinely improvise rescue efforts, even within the megalopolis of Cairo.
Fire escapes, smoke detectors and alarms are rare and in many areas, warrens of narrow roads make it hard for fire engines to reach disaster sites.
Car crashes are also common, and often blamed on reckless driving, poor maintenance and uneven law enforcement, with traffic laws also being widely flouted.
Last year, nearly 6,000 people died in road accidents across the country, according to Egypt’s state statistics agency.
The year before, more than 5,200 road deaths were recorded across the country.
In August, at least 18 people, many of them teenagers, were killed in northern Egypt when two pickup trucks carrying agricultural day-labourers crashed.

title_en: US finds no evidence China told Alice Huang to spy on Nvidia’s Jensen Huang, report says
content_en:
US officials say Alice Huang contacted China’s spy agency during the affair but found ⁠no indication ⁠she provided significant intelligence.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang speaks with Alice Huang in Taipei, Taiwan, in June 2024. Photo: Reuters
US ⁠officials found no evidence ⁠that tech executive Alice Huang was directed by Beijing to spy on Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, The Wall Street Journal reported on Wednesday, citing people familiar with a classified briefing.
The briefing ‌comes after US President Donald Trump cleared the way for Jensen Huang’s reinstatement earlier this week, assuring Nvidia that its CEO posed no national-security threat.
The controversy began with concerns over Alice Huang’s alleged Chinese intelligence links and whether her relationship with Jensen Huang affected suspected diversions ⁠of Nvidia chips to China.
Officials from the CIA, FBI, Office of the Director ‌of National Intelligence and National Security Agency briefed staff from congressional intelligence committees and chamber leaders, the Journal reported.
The officials said ‌Alice Huang contacted China’s spy agency during the affair but found ⁠no indication ⁠that she provided significant intelligence, the Journal reported.
[embedded media]
Nvidia and the agencies did not immediately respond ‌to a request for comment. Reuters could not independently verify the report.
Shares of Nvidia tumbled more ‌than 7 per cent, ‌putting the chipmaker on track to shed more than US$250 billion in ‌market value and eroding a 31 per cent comeback rally after CEO Huang’s reinstatement that ⁠added over US$900 billion.
The report said current evidence suggests that Alice Huang and Jensen ⁠Huang may have had an amorous relationship, but not a coordinated play by China, adding that new information could, however, change that ‌assessment.
The briefing also noted ‌that Kang Wei, described to the Journal as Alice Huang’s husband by people who know them, was an asset for China’s Ministry of State Security who remained in frequent contact with the intelligence service.

title_en: China’s tech ambitions to stay on track despite Shanghai party chief’s ouster: analysts
content_en:
Projects tied to ousted Shanghai Communist Party chief may face reviews, but country’s broader AI and chip push expected to remain intact.
An AI sign is seen at the World Artificial Intelligence Conference in Shanghai. Photo: Reuters
The ousting of Shanghai Communist Party chief Chen Jining, a prominent technocrat who championed the city’s artificial intelligence and semiconductor sectors, could heighten scrutiny of state-backed tech investments, although analysts see little sign of a shift in China’s broader tech ambitions.
State media reported on Tuesday that Chen, 62, a Politburo member once tipped for higher office, had been placed under investigation for suspected “serious breaches of discipline and law” – a common euphemism for corruption.
He is the fourth member of the ruling party’s elite decision-making body to come under investigation since the current term began in 2022, a rate unseen in decades.
“His downfall could surely create short-term political uncertainty around projects and firms most closely associated with his personal backing, particularly those that received visible support from Shanghai during his tenure,” said Qiu Mingda, a senior analyst at political risk consultancy Eurasia Group.
Qiu said Chen had played an important political role in backing Shanghai’s push into AI and chips, using his endorsements and coordination to accelerate policy implementation and mobilise local state capital.
Decisions linked to those investments would now face greater scrutiny, Qiu added, pointing out that AI supply chain firms granted expedited initial public offerings under Chen’s tenure could also come under review.
A former president of Tsinghua University who also served as environment minister and mayor of Beijing, Chen took the helm of China’s premier financial hub in 2022 and quickly accelerated its push to become a global AI powerhouse.
During his tenure, Chen actively courted foreign tech executives, hosting Tesla CEO Elon Musk in 2023 and Apple chairman Tim Cook last month, when he urged the US giant to “make full use of Shanghai’s strengths”. Last year, he also accompanied President Xi Jinping on an inspection tour of a local AI hub.
In July, Shanghai’s municipal party committee approved a policy road map aimed at turning the city into a centre for AI innovation and governance. Chen called for breakthroughs in foundational technologies, stronger financial backing and expanded computing clusters.
There’s no reason to believe there is any big policy shiftRui Ma, Tech Buzz China
The city hosts the annual World Artificial Intelligence Conference – China’s premier AI showcase – and is home to prominent AI developers MiniMax and StepFun, as well as Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corporation (SMIC), China’s largest contract chipmaker.
Still, Rui Ma, a tech analyst and founder of the Tech Buzz China newsletter, said Shanghai’s tech ecosystem had already possessed deep structural strengths before Chen’s arrival.
“There’s no reason to believe there is any big policy shift,” she said.
While specific deals approved during Chen’s tenure could be reviewed if the investigation exposed corruption or misused funds, Ma said she did not expect the probe to derail Shanghai’s ambitions or China’s national strategies for AI and deep tech.
Su Lian Jye, chief analyst at consultancy Omdia, shared that view, saying that while Chen amplified the city’s strengths and projected an “open for business” image to foreign investors, China’s technological and economic advances were never dependent on a single individual.
“As such, Chen’s departure is unlikely to derail Shanghai’s technology development,” Su said, noting that AI and semiconductors were embedded in China’s five-year plan and backed by clear central government directives.
“While local execution may be affected, the policies will remain in place to ensure strict adherence to central directives.”
Shanghai’s municipal party leadership reiterated its commitment to national strategic priorities at a meeting held immediately after Chen’s probe was announced.
The main things to watch are personnel changes in Shanghai, any reassessment of state-backed investments, and signs that local officials have become more risk-averse in approving or advancing projectsQiu Mingda, Eurasia Group
Central authorities have also maintained their aggressive infrastructure targets.
In September, the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology unveiled a plan targeting 9,800 exaflops of intelligent computing capacity by 2030, backed by 3.8 trillion yuan (US$570 billion) in cumulative information infrastructure investment between 2026 and 2030.
Still, the political shock has coincided with a broader sell-off in Chinese tech shares.
On Wednesday – the first trading day after the investigation into Chen was announced – the benchmark Shanghai Composite Index fell 2 per cent, with semiconductor stocks tumbling 7.9 per cent.
In Hong Kong, the Hang Seng Tech Index dropped 2.6 per cent, dragged down by sharp losses among Shanghai-based chip firms: Biren Technology, Iluvatar CoreX and Hua Hong fell 24.7 per cent, 18.5 per cent and 17.3 per cent, respectively, while AI model developer MiniMax tumbled 13.8 per cent and SMIC lost 7.6 per cent.
Markets partially recovered on Thursday, with mainland Chinese and Hong Kong tech stocks recouping some of their losses.
Ma cautioned against attributing any further cooling in AI funding solely to Chen’s downfall, saying funding activity had already been moderating for months due to a mismatch between investor expectations and commercial realities.
For tech firms and investors, Qiu said the most immediate risks lay in policy execution rather than policy direction, particularly in the form of potential delays, reviews and greater caution among local officials.
Semiconductor projects in Shanghai’s industrial hubs could face “added political sensitivity if they were closely linked to Chen’s support”, he said.
“The main things to watch are personnel changes in Shanghai, any reassessment of state-backed investments, and signs that local officials have become more risk-averse in approving or advancing projects.”
By Chong Ming Lee

title_en: Why Xi’s warning against a ‘blind’ tech rush is suddenly ringing louder
content_en:
Official commentary says some local authorities that rushed to secure land for data centres have bought chips that are not up to the job.
An AI trainer operates a robot to collect data at a humanoid robot innovation centre in Wuhan, Hubei province, this month. Photo: Xinhua
Chinese President Xi Jinping’s warning last month against a disorderly rush into new industries has come into sharper focus this week with an investigation into Shanghai’s party chief, a sell-off in chip stocks and renewed questions about whether China’s computing boom can pay for itself.
During an October 16 visit to Ulanqab, a computing hub in north China’s Inner Mongolia autonomous region, Xi cautioned against blind competition and development that ignored local conditions.
Then on Wednesday, Study Times, an official publication run by the Central Party School, invoked Xi’s remarks in a commentary piece warning that some localities had rushed to secure land and resources and bought chips without adequately assessing customers’ needs.
The commentary appeared a day after authorities announced that Shanghai party secretary Chen Jining was under investigation for suspected serious violations of discipline and law. Chen, who is also a member of the powerful Politburo, is widely seen as a pro-tech policymaker who encourages support for innovation companies. The investigation notice did not identify any companies.
Study Times’ commentary said some artificial intelligence (AI) computing centres built by local-government-backed companies had bought mid- and low-end chips that were unable to keep pace with evolving large AI models, even as advanced computing power remained scarce.
Projects that failed to attract business would struggle to recoup construction, maintenance, depreciation and power costs, putting sustained pressure on local state-owned capital and potentially creating financial risks, the commentary said.
“Building computing centres is not difficult; the difficulty lies in putting them to use,” the piece said, adding that the nationwide rack occupancy rate at the end of June was 71.4 per cent.
It argued that markets should determine how resources were allocated.
The commentary came amid a sell-off in chip stocks as investors gauge the impact of Chen’s investigation.
On Wednesday – the first trading day after the investigation into Chen was announced – Hong Kong-listed Shanghai Biren Technology, Iluvatar CoreX and Hua Hong fell 24.7 per cent, 18.5 per cent and 17.3 per cent, respectively.
US asset manager KraneShares said in a Wednesday commentary that Chen’s investigation had contributed to losses in Hong Kong and mainland China alongside broader weakness in Asia’s AI supply chain.
The firm described Chen as a supporter of Shanghai’s development and the city’s AI and technology industries.
However, “Beijing’s supportive technology policies do not appear to be going anywhere,” KraneShares wrote.
Building computing centres is not difficult; the difficulty lies in putting them to useStudy Times
Research firm SemiAnalysis said in a report released in September that older, low-density data centres were often physically unsuitable for AI servers and were costly to retrofit. That legacy stock helped explain why high vacancy rates could coexist with shortages of suitable AI infrastructure, it said.
The scale of China’s data centre expansion raises the stakes. At a briefing in July, the National Development and Reform Commission cited estimates of 4 trillion yuan (about US$600 billion) in new computing-network investment between 2026 and 2030, while urging projects to be matched to demand.
Local government debt remains a long-standing concern for China’s economy. Official figures put hidden local government debt at 14.3 trillion yuan at the end of 2023 and 6.5 trillion yuan at the end of 2025. Beijing has been replacing such liabilities with official local government bonds to ease repayment pressure.
By Howard Liu

An AI trainer operates a robot to collect data at a humanoid robot innovation centre in Wuhan, Hubei province, this month. Photo: Xinhua
Chinese President Xi Jinping’s warning last month against a disorderly rush into new industries has come into sharper focus this week with an investigation into Shanghai’s party chief, a sell-off in chip stocks and renewed questions about whether China’s computing boom can pay for itself.
During an October 16 visit to Ulanqab, a computing hub in north China’s Inner Mongolia autonomous region, Xi cautioned against blind competition and development that ignored local conditions.
Then on Wednesday, Study Times, an official publication run by the Central Party School, invoked Xi’s remarks in a commentary piece warning that some localities had rushed to secure land and resources and bought chips without adequately assessing customers’ needs.
The commentary appeared a day after authorities announced that Shanghai party secretary Chen Jining was under investigation for suspected serious violations of discipline and law. Chen, who is also a member of the powerful Politburo, is widely seen as a pro-tech policymaker who encourages support for innovation companies. The investigation notice did not identify any companies.
Study Times’ commentary said some artificial intelligence (AI) computing centres built by local-government-backed companies had bought mid- and low-end chips that were unable to keep pace with evolving large AI models, even as advanced computing power remained scarce.
Projects that failed to attract business would struggle to recoup construction, maintenance, depreciation and power costs, putting sustained pressure on local state-owned capital and potentially creating financial risks, the commentary said.
“Building computing centres is not difficult; the difficulty lies in putting them to use,” the piece said, adding that the nationwide rack occupancy rate at the end of June was 71.4 per cent.
It argued that markets should determine how resources were allocated.
The commentary came amid a sell-off in chip stocks as investors gauge the impact of Chen’s investigation.
On Wednesday – the first trading day after the investigation into Chen was announced – Hong Kong-listed Shanghai Biren Technology, Iluvatar CoreX and Hua Hong fell 24.7 per cent, 18.5 per cent and 17.3 per cent, respectively.
US asset manager KraneShares said in a Wednesday commentary that Chen’s investigation had contributed to losses in Hong Kong and mainland China alongside broader weakness in Asia’s AI supply chain.
The firm described Chen as a supporter of Shanghai’s development and the city’s AI and technology industries.
However, “Beijing’s supportive technology policies do not appear to be going anywhere,” KraneShares wrote.
Building computing centres is not difficult; the difficulty lies in putting them to useStudy Times
Research firm SemiAnalysis said in a report released in September that older, low-density data centres were often physically unsuitable for AI servers and were costly to retrofit. That legacy stock helped explain why high vacancy rates could coexist with shortages of suitable AI infrastructure, it said.
The scale of China’s data centre expansion raises the stakes. At a briefing in July, the National Development and Reform Commission cited estimates of 4 trillion yuan (about US$600 billion) in new computing-network investment between 2026 and 2030, while urging projects to be matched to demand.
Local government debt remains a long-standing concern for China’s economy. Official figures put hidden local government debt at 14.3 trillion yuan at the end of 2023 and 6.5 trillion yuan at the end of 2025. Beijing has been replacing such liabilities with official local government bonds to ease repayment pressure.
By Howard Liu

title_en: Huawei advances home-grown chip design ecosystem while eyeing global push to rival Nvidia
content_en:
Huawei is working with local chip designers, foundries and packaging firms to achieve large-scale production for its Tau projects.
The Huawei logo displayed at the World Artificial Intelligence Conference in Shanghai, July 17, 2026. Photo: Reuters
Huawei Technologies and a local software partner claim to have made breakthroughs in domestic chip design tools built around the telecoms equipment giant’s Tau Scaling Law, marking the latest effort to cultivate a self-reliant semiconductor supply chain in China.
Hangzhou-based Phlexing Technology said at Huawei’s annual intellectual property (IP) event in Beijing on Tuesday that it had partnered with the Shenzhen-based company to develop extraction and sign-off tools for electronic design automation (EDA) software – key steps in producing chips under the Tau framework.
In what Phlexing chairman He Qing described as an industry first, Huawei linked Phlexing’s tools with other home-grown EDA software to create “an interoperable domestic toolchain”.
Huawei also coordinated chip designers, foundries and packaging firms across the local supply chain to achieve large-scale production for its Tau chip projects, according to He.
“Tau EDA, the domestic toolset designed for Tau chips, was forged through years of deep collaboration with Huawei,” He said, noting that the software translated the theoretical Tau Scaling Law into “quantifiable and verifiable engineering capabilities”.
People visit an exhibition during Huawei Connect 2026 in Shanghai on September 17. Photo: AFP
He said the tape-out of a large batch of Huawei chips had demonstrated the software’s capabilities in real-world production.
The claims underscore Huawei’s drive to overcome US export controls on advanced chipmaking tools.
First unveiled in May alongside its LogicFolding architecture, the Tau Scaling Law is a design principle that Huawei said could deliver transistor performance equivalent to a 1.4-nanometre process node by 2031 without relying on advanced lithography tools which are restricted from export to China.
Rather than shrinking physical chip sizes, the framework focuses on time compression and system-level architectural efficiency.
Alongside its domestic hardware push, Huawei is also reorganising its IP operations to support an overseas expansion of its computing ecosystem to rival Nvidia’s.
Chief IP officer Alan Fan told the South China Morning Post on the sidelines of Tuesday’s event that Huawei had created IP teams for semiconductors and artificial intelligence, transferring engineers from research and development departments to staff the new units.
The move supports Huawei’s efforts to take large-scale computing systems – such as the Ascend-powered Atlas 950 SuperPoD introduced in March – to international markets, where it is promoting its Cann software platform as an alternative to Nvidia’s dominant Cuda ecosystem.
Achieving full self-sufficiency at home, however, requires overcoming a critical bottleneck in EDA software – a sector long dominated by US-based Synopsys, Cadence Design Systems and Siemens EDA.
While those foreign giants offer end-to-end, integrated ecosystems, Chinese vendors have traditionally only handled isolated steps of the design process, lacking a complete “full-flow” digital solution.
Other domestic players are also rallying around Huawei’s architecture to close that gap. In June, major Chinese EDA provider Empyrean Technology launched Argus, a physical verification platform for three-dimensional integrated circuits that the company described as “a key carrier” for implementing the Tau framework.
Additional reporting by Howard Liu
By Iris Deng

title_en: How US-China tech rivalry has been reset by Jensen Huang saga
content_en:
Gavekal Technologies’ Laila Khawaja says heightened scrutiny of Nvidia and its boss could bring China’s AI firms short-term pain but long-term gain from self-sufficiency.
Illustration: Lau Ka-kuen
Laila Khawaja is research director at Gavekal Technologies, the financial services and analytics firm’s tech wing. Before her current role, she worked at Gavekal Fathom China from its founding in 2009, developing broad expertise in China’s corporate landscape. A graduate of Beijing Foreign Studies University and Harvard University, she is currently based in Miami.
In this interview, Khawaja discusses the whirlwind dismissal and restoration of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, how that saga and other recent events have reframed the US-China tech rivalry and what is frequently misunderstood about each side’s strengths and weaknesses in the global artificial intelligence race.
This interview first appeared in SCMP Plus. For other interviews in the Open Questions series, click here.
Do you see the recent saga around Nvidia as a turning point for the China-US tech competition? Why or why not?
Yes and no. In the near term, the saga will have a significant impact on the competitive dynamics. Jensen Huang is the single most influential advocate for looser technology controls on China. Even with his reinstatement, he is unlikely to continue his advocacy due to intensified scrutiny and potential political backlash. The trajectory for US export controls on China is only going to be more hawkish, and we are already seeing the impact.
We have seen the release of the latest [US Bureau of Industry and Security] remote access rule, and the blacklist of [Singaporean cloud computing firm] Megaspeed and its related entities.
The new BIS rule targets not only China’s remote access to advanced AI computing power – which is expected to account for about one-third of China’s cumulative AI compute access by 2027 – but also diversion and Chinese AI chip designers’ access to overseas foundries. Its impact is therefore much broader than the headlines suggest.
If BIS strictly enforces the rule, including by declining many licences for access, China’s AI sector could suffer significant near-term pain because many doors to advanced AI computing power would effectively be shut.
Chinese companies would have little choice but to rely on their existing stock of restricted chips and domestic production. Supply through both channels is quite limited.
However, I do not think the Nvidia saga changes the long-term direction of US-China AI or technology competition. China’s push for semiconductor self-sufficiency has been under way for many years.
For Beijing, reducing reliance on foreign technology and building an indigenous Chinese technology stack has almost always been a priority – arguably as important as seeing Chinese AI labs dominate global benchmarks.
Before the Nvidia saga, Chinese AI companies preferred foreign chips because they were better. There was a degree of misalignment between the government’s priorities and what the companies wanted.
Now, with the saga and new restrictions, Chinese companies may have fewer fantasies about continued access to foreign chips and will more fully embrace domestic alternatives.
This will only accelerate the development of the domestic tech stack, because it will lead to more user feedback and kick off a positive feedback loop that helps them improve.
[embedded media]
What does Huang’s departure and comeback mean for global AI demand?
Huang is certainly irreplaceable and highly influential in the global AI sector. His comeback is good for Nvidia’s business and the global AI sector, but it does not resolve ongoing concerns over AI’s return on investment, circular financing, rising cost of capital or the changing political environment after the midterms.
One big variable is the new BIS remote-access rule.
If BIS enforces it very strictly, a lot of Chinese remote access to computing power could be cut off. We need to see whether those freed-up compute resources are easily reallocated.
[US President Donald Trump] has also made some bold claims on blocking US companies from building AI data centres overseas and imposing hefty taxes on firms that do so. This is contradictory to his diffusionist approach – but it’s Trump. If he does so, it will be really bad for US hyperscalers, as global diffusion is important if the US objective is to secure global leadership in AI before China catches up.
Compounded by the Democratic “blue wave”, we might see some slowdown in data centre buildouts and more market consolidation. However, that isn’t necessarily a bad thing – more disciplined, paced investment can be healthy for the industry in the long run.
If consolidation removes weaker players and weaker projects, it could also give US power infrastructure more time to catch up. Some estimates suggest that power constraints could become a serious bottleneck for US data-centre construction in late 2027 and 2028.
Another factor is US-China AI competition. Regardless of what happens in the US, the Chinese government remains firmly committed to developing AI.
Beijing appears to believe that AI is a transformative technology that can boost productivity, and it wants to diffuse AI across the economy and globally.
Competition between the US and China will give both countries strong incentives to sustain investment in AI.
[embedded media]
Does the new BIS rule change the nature of export controls?
I see the recent BIS rule less as a fundamental shift in the US approach and more as a very serious effort to close a loophole in existing export controls.
The US began limiting exports of advanced AI chips to China in October 2022, which focused on physical chips. However, until the latest BIS rule, remote access was considered legal.
That created an obvious policy gap. If Washington’s stated goal is to limit China’s access to advanced computing power, it does not make sense to limit physical chip exports while leaving the door wide open to remote access to those same chips.
My interpretation is that this contradiction was not necessarily the result of a calculated policy choice. It reflected incoherent policymaking in Washington and loopholes in the existing US export-control framework.
This was already a well-recognised loophole within Washington; Congress had been trying to close it since April 2024, when they first introduced the Remote Access Security Act.
So this whole Nvidia saga basically just added political urgency and accelerated that policy effort.
What does the new rule reveal about divisions in Washington?
There are two layers to the issue. One is potential corruption and knowing violations of export controls. There have been constant suspicions and speculation that improper business dealings or corruption may have been involved in the administration.
In my view, that is plausible, and we will find out more through the ongoing investigations.
The other layer is the debate over export controls themselves.
Export controls are difficult to calibrate. If they are too loose, they can give rivals the technology they need to improve their competitiveness and military capabilities, potentially threatening national security.
But if controls are too restrictive, they can hurt the revenue of domestic companies and potentially weaken their ability to invest in research and development. They can also incentivise rivals to double down on innovation and develop alternative systems.
Trump officials and tech CEOs have been divided on this export control debate regarding advanced chips.
On one side, you have the hawks advocating for tighter controls on national security grounds; on the other, you have Trump, Huang and [White House adviser] David Sacks advocating for diffusing the American tech stack globally to secure American technological leadership, market share and global influence.
They believe that maintaining global influence will deter rivals such as Huawei Technologies from developing highly competitive alternative systems.
The middle ground they reached was permitting the export of the H200, which was Nvidia’s third- or fourth-best chip. But the Nvidia saga, which involved remote access and chip diversion, complicated that debate.
The export controls did not work as intended. What I want to highlight is that this debate between control and diffusion is highly legitimate and not unique to Washington.
As China ascends in various tech sectors, the Chinese government is also releasing technology export controls, and we can see from policy documents that Beijing is wrestling with the same balancing act.
[embedded media]
Is the “small yard, high fence” expanding?
The yard is certainly getting bigger and the fence is getting higher. The problem is that the boundary is difficult to draw, because national security is a very broadly defined concept.
In export controls, I think the focus will gradually shift from restricting access to advanced chips – an area where the US has already done a great deal – to controls on semiconductor manufacturing equipment.
The argument is that if controls on equipment are looser than controls on the chips themselves, they will simply enable China to manufacture its own chips. That would undermine the purpose of the restrictions.
The US has already been implementing pretty strict equipment controls since 2022, though there are still loopholes in the framework.
The bill to watch very closely will be the Match Act, which would force US allies to align with US export controls, with a special focus on advanced lithography machines from [Dutch equipment maker] ASML.
That bill would have major consequences because it would not only restrict more tool exports, but also potentially suspend components and services for existing advanced lithography systems, which would have a very damaging impact on China’s existing production capacity of advanced chips.
There is also a parallel concern in the US regarding Chinese products and components in US communications networks, infrastructure and supply chains.
The [US Federal Communications Commission] has been spearheading quite a bit of restriction there, targeting a wide range of Chinese imports.
We’re talking about things like drones, robots and power inverters, and now there is discussion about potentially blocking optical transceivers.
The FCC’s concerns revolve around data security, cybersecurity and over-reliance on Chinese supply chains, which they believe pose a significant national security threat.
Just as China is pursuing self-sufficiency, the US is pursuing very similar goals in strategic sectors.
Of course, there is a disconnect between policy ambitions and practical reality for both sides, but the trend of strategic decoupling at this point is irreversible.
How effective have US technology controls been?
The impact of these controls has been uneven, as the control regime on advanced-chip exports has proved quite porous because of remote access and chip diversion.
But one point I want to emphasise: even though China has continued to gain access through these channels, the restrictions have raised costs for Chinese AI companies and supply remains limited.
As a result, we are seeing greater adoption of domestic chips. That is helping domestic products improve.
Compute constraints have also encouraged innovation in China in areas such as algorithms, model architecture, inference efficiency and compute-cluster management, because Chinese companies need to operate different types of chips within the same cluster and need to maximise utilisation of limited compute resources.
That progress will enhance the competitiveness of China’s technology stack.
However, controls on high-bandwidth memory (HBM) and semiconductor manufacturing equipment have created much greater challenges for China, because they directly affect China’s ability to expand onshore advanced chip manufacturing capacity.
Domestic HBM production is also constrained to a large extent by these tool restrictions. While these restrictions have certainly created fresh opportunities for domestic toolmakers – and Chinese toolmakers are indeed making progress in certain categories – many critical gaps remain.
I would caution against a common analogy between China’s semiconductor catch-up and its success in electric vehicles.
Advanced semiconductor manufacturing is perhaps the single most complex and globalised industrial process in the world, involving more than a thousand complex process steps and requiring hundreds of advanced tools to work reliably together.
The constraint isn’t just lithography, which always grabs the headlines; it spans a wide range of different tools, software and know-how. Foreign incumbents have spent decades accumulating this technology, know-how, IP and reliability track record.
So while I am confident in China’s ability to eventually make a breakthrough, I believe it will be a very lengthy and capital-intensive process.
[embedded media]
Can opposition from US allies weaken the Match Act?
The Dutch government and ASML have consistently opposed tighter controls on the export of lithography machines to China. Under US pressure, however, the Dutch government agreed to restrictions on ASML’s advanced immersion-lithography systems.
My view is that opposition from the Dutch government as well as from ASML is unlikely to be the deciding factor. These parties have limited leverage.
Ultimately, the outcome will depend on Washington’s own assessment of the controls and on China’s response.
What is the outlook on tech after the US midterm elections?
I am not an expert on US politics, but I can share my views.
The various export controls on China have had bipartisan support. It is not just the Democrats; there is support across both parties.
The main people slowing these controls were Trump and a small number of his officials, as well as Jensen Huang and his lobbying efforts, because they were not fully on board for a variety of reasons.
My reading of the midterms is that China is not the central issue for Democrats. Their priorities are more likely to be affordability and inflation, investigating potential corruption in the Trump administration, ending the Iran war and ending the Russia-Ukraine war.
After January, however, I think the single biggest variable to watch will be the outcome of the investigations into Nvidia and Huang. Trump’s personal intervention to reinstate Huang as CEO has already invigorated the hawks and Democrats.
If the investigations uncover corruption or questionable business dealings within the administration, or serious export-control violations by Nvidia or Huang, that would almost certainly inject fresh momentum into a more hawkish US technology policy towards China. We could expect even tighter controls.
Will scrutiny spread to AMD and other US chipmakers?
Broadly speaking, the Nvidia saga is likely to attract fresh scrutiny of American companies with ties to China. Those ties could be personal or commercial, and investigators may examine whether business dealings are questionable.
In the semiconductor sector, the key question is whether there has been any transfer of technology or products, including chips, in violation of US export controls. There may also be other business dealings that are considered sensitive or impermissible under US rules.
AMD is an obvious target for scrutiny. I am not sure that this is because of personal ties. A more likely reason is that AMD is the second choice for Chinese buyers seeking advanced AI chips.
I had a quick skim of the original short-seller report. I think it contains some errors. AMD’s revenue in China does not come exclusively from AI chips. The company also sells a substantial amount of CPU products there. Those errors raise questions about the report’s credibility.
I would also highlight that, shortly after China shut the door on Nvidia’s H200, AMD held a high-profile event involving its China business. It even advertised itself as “Advanced Mutual Development” at the event. AMD is clearly trying to capture some of the market share Nvidia has lost.
But that is not proof that AMD has done anything wrong. The Trump administration approved the export of some AMD chips to China.
Based on what I have heard from people on the ground, I have not heard of AMD chips being diverted. They are also not as desirable to Chinese buyers as Nvidia’s chips.
Where are China’s biggest vulnerabilities in AI and semiconductors?
Start with semiconductors. China can design chips, so chip design is not really the problem. It can also develop world-leading AI models, as we have already seen.
The constraint is advanced computing power, which is very important because data, algorithms and computing power are the three key elements of AI.
Now that the door to foreign chips is basically shut, hopes rest on domestic production. But I would describe the bottleneck as a whole-supply-chain problem for the advanced semiconductor stack.
China’s self-sufficiency across the entire stack – ranging from advanced tools and their critical components to advanced semiconductor materials, electronic design automation tools and packaging – still depends heavily on foreign technologies and suppliers.
As for the AI stack, China has done a very good job in algorithmic innovation, inference efficiency and cost management.
China also claims to have a major advantage in data because it has a huge manufacturing base and many industries operating domestically.
That creates data availability. But Chinese industrial data is often fragmented and not standardised, so it is not necessarily ready for model training.
That is why the Chinese government is orchestrating a top-down effort to collect and organise high-quality data sets. If that effort succeeds, China could have a considerable advantage in this area.
Monetisation is definitely important. Data is expensive, and AI compute, safety testing and experimental research are expensive.
Given the current technology sell-off and the persistent monetisation challenges facing Chinese AI models, the question of how these companies will generate returns is an important one.
How are Chinese AI companies monetising their technology?
Monetisation is different for hyperscalers such as ByteDance and [South China Morning Post owner] Alibaba, compared with independent AI labs. For independent labs, their main revenue sources are local deployment services or application programming interfaces (APIs).
Looking at the financials of listed labs, they are deriving an increasing proportion of their revenue from overseas. The question is whether that overseas revenue is sustainable given the new controls.
Even with overseas sales, their API revenue remains very small compared with the US frontier labs, raising the question of whether they can generate enough revenue to recover their costs.
For the hyperscalers like ByteDance, it’s a two-part story.
First, they incorporate AI into internal business to improve efficiency and generate more revenue, including through e-commerce and advertising.
Second, companies like ByteDance and Alibaba pursue a full-stack strategy offering cloud services, leveraging their compute resources to provide models-as-a-service.
Alibaba’s earnings have already shown that the margins from providing its own models and third-party models are very similar. As long as a company has computing resources, it can monetise them.
The other area is stand-alone AI applications. There is still limited evidence that these applications can generate sufficient revenue.
That is due to several factors, including consumers’ low willingness to pay in China and intense competition among companies, with subsidies and price competition.
One bright spot is video generation models, particularly from ByteDance, which benefit from vertical integration across content distribution and video models.
They have done well, though a major downstream application of video models – microdramas – is becoming extremely cutthroat and crowded. So there are still questions about how sustainable that growth is going forward.
Lastly, revenue could come from AI hardware. China has a very strong manufacturing supply chain and cost advantage.
It can produce hardware at scale and add AI capabilities to it. There could be decent opportunities if China can produce attractive AI hardware.
Just like in other manufacturing sectors, even if the domestic market doesn’t generate high margins, companies can export overseas where there is plenty of demand. That’s definitely a space to watch.
[embedded media]
Which country is better positioned to export its AI stack globally?
The practical problem is that China does not yet have a complete AI stack that it can export at scale because it lacks advanced chips.
Even if Chinese models are adopted, they often run on US chips, including in [Belt and Road Initiative] countries. That is still a significant disadvantage.
China’s limited onshore production of advanced chips will remain a substantial bottleneck to diffusing its AI stack in the near term, and that likely won’t be resolved in the next two to three years.
Furthermore, with the crackdown on model distillation and remote access, there are questions about how fast Chinese models can continue advancing.
Chinese companies can still generate revenue by providing local deployment services for smaller models running on existing hardware, but in the near term, as long as the US continues to push global diffusion, the US is likely to hold the upper hand.
Can China eventually replace advanced US chips?
All these challenges and workarounds come down to the same fundamental issue: chip manufacturing.
Even if you use a supernode architecture to compensate for lower single-chip performance by networking many chips together, you still need a massive volume of chips, so it again comes down to chip manufacturing.
You can design these architectures on paper and in theory, but the real test is whether you can mass-produce them in volume using reliable equipment in a profitable manner.
Profitability is secondary here – the core question is mass production, which brings us right back to China’s lag in advanced semiconductor equipment.
Catching up in equipment isn’t easy. Beyond technology and know-how, you face strict IP walls, and even after building a tool, it takes at least two to three years of reliability testing to achieve the desired yields.
So there are no quick short cuts in moving forward. However, because of these constraints, China will definitely double down on exploring all alternative pathways, and by concentrating a whole-of-nation effort, it may eventually find breakthroughs.
Where could China make the biggest breakthroughs in semiconductor equipment?
In equipment, China may have a better chance of making progress in areas where demand is greatest.
For instance, etching, deposition and hybrid bonding tools. There are still substantial gaps, but these tools are needed for multiple critical applications, so China may be able to mobilise more resources and effort. There are also some good Chinese companies in these areas.
Breakthroughs in advanced lithography, particularly extreme ultraviolet lithography, will be extremely difficult. Inspection and metrology equipment will also be very tough nuts to crack.
Does China have an energy advantage in AI?
I think China’s energy advantage in AI is somewhat overstated.
Energy is very important. China’s power grid is the world’s largest and one of its most advanced, and it continues to add generation capacity.
But China’s electricity advantage is not so much about the cost of electricity; it is about the availability of energy.
[embedded media]
Another point that is often misunderstood is the share of electricity in data-centre costs.
Electricity accounts for about one-quarter of the annual operating expenditure of a US data centre.
But if you factor in both operating expenditure and capital expenditure, electricity accounts for only about 7 per cent of the all-in annual cost of a US data centre.
So even if China has an overwhelming advantage in electricity costs, that may not matter as much as people think.
The bulk of the all-in cost – around 60 per cent – is the servers, where China does not have an advantage.
That said, power availability will matter a great deal if the US hits grid bottlenecks.
We could end up with a very interesting dynamic in the coming years: China builds plenty of data centres with abundant power, waiting on advanced chips, while the US has plenty of advanced chips, waiting on power.
How effective are China’s rare earth countermeasures?
Trump’s claim [of catching up with China in rare earth in 10 months] is highly exaggerated.
Rare earths have genuinely been China’s trump card, and their potency will last well into the foreseeable future.
Even though we are seeing concerted efforts by the US and its allies to build alternative supply chains, that will be a very lengthy process.
Japan is probably the best example. Even after about 15 years of effort, Japan – a technologically advanced country – has only reduced its dependence on China for rare earth imports from around 90 per cent in 2010 to about 65 to 70 per cent today.
This shows that while China’s leverage may diminish gradually over time, substantially eliminating it is a multi-decade endeavour.
A realistic assessment for the US is that it could achieve high self-sufficiency in rare earths for the defence sector within two to three years, since defence volumes are relatively small.
However, it is likely to take 10 years or more for the US to reduce its dependence on Chinese rare earths across broader civilian sectors.
That matters enormously because we are talking about critical materials used across countless civilian applications, including the semiconductor industry itself.
Unlike US export controls on chips and equipment, China’s dominance in rare earths can have an immediate effect on global supply chains. China has been approving export licences selectively and incrementally, using that process to extend its leverage.
So far, that approach appears to have worked, as we have seen in the back-and-forth in bilateral relations.
Is there room for understanding in the US-China technology trade?
Strategic decoupling is mutual and is an irreversible trend, as we have discussed. Both sides are working to reduce their strategic dependence on each other.
But there is certainly room to reach some kind of consensus to maintain stability during this period – what’s been called “constructive strategic stability”.
The problem is that, although we have learned that escalation is not sustainable, there appears to be a persistent underestimation in Washington of China’s ability and willingness to retaliate.
Perhaps US policymakers will need to experience more rounds of escalation before they learn that lesson.
The Match Act will be a good test. China has already vowed to retaliate, and I think it will do so because of the impact the legislation could have.
We will see how that plays out, and perhaps it will bring the discussion back to constructive strategic stability.
What’s the export outlook for Chinese AI commercial applications and less advanced chips?
Commercial applications are complicated because of data-security concerns.
We have already seen how those issues played out in the TikTok dispute. It depends on the application and its nature. Video-editing applications, for example, may be treated differently.
There are already Chinese video-editing apps available in the US, whereas an app such as TikTok may not be acceptable. It will be assessed case by case, depending on data security and concerns about propaganda.
As for mature semiconductors, I think this is an area that will attract growing scrutiny from the US.
China is expanding its production capacity very quickly, largely without the equipment export controls that apply to advanced manufacturing.
China’s share of global mature-chip production capacity is expected to rise from about one-third in 2024 to more than half by 2030.
This matters because, although mature chips do not require advanced process technology, they are widely used in both defence and non-defence applications. Mature semiconductors account for more than 90 per cent of global chip sales by volume.
It is therefore almost inevitable that the US will increase scrutiny of this area, given China’s potential leverage to disrupt global supply chains.
