title_display: How US-China tech rivalry has been reset by Jensen Huang saga
content_display:
Gavekal Technologies’ Laila Khawaja says heightened scrutiny of Nvidia and its boss could bring China’s AI firms short-term pain but long-term gain from self-sufficiency.
Illustration: Lau Ka-kuen
Laila Khawaja is research director at Gavekal Technologies, the financial services and analytics firm’s tech wing. Before her current role, she worked at Gavekal Fathom China from its founding in 2009, developing broad expertise in China’s corporate landscape. A graduate of Beijing Foreign Studies University and Harvard University, she is currently based in Miami.
In this interview, Khawaja discusses the whirlwind dismissal and restoration of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, how that saga and other recent events have reframed the US-China tech rivalry and what is frequently misunderstood about each side’s strengths and weaknesses in the global artificial intelligence race.
This interview first appeared in SCMP Plus. For other interviews in the Open Questions series, click here.
Do you see the recent saga around Nvidia as a turning point for the China-US tech competition? Why or why not?
Yes and no. In the near term, the saga will have a significant impact on the competitive dynamics. Jensen Huang is the single most influential advocate for looser technology controls on China. Even with his reinstatement, he is unlikely to continue his advocacy due to intensified scrutiny and potential political backlash. The trajectory for US export controls on China is only going to be more hawkish, and we are already seeing the impact.
We have seen the release of the latest [US Bureau of Industry and Security] remote access rule, and the blacklist of [Singaporean cloud computing firm] Megaspeed and its related entities.
The new BIS rule targets not only China’s remote access to advanced AI computing power – which is expected to account for about one-third of China’s cumulative AI compute access by 2027 – but also diversion and Chinese AI chip designers’ access to overseas foundries. Its impact is therefore much broader than the headlines suggest.
If BIS strictly enforces the rule, including by declining many licences for access, China’s AI sector could suffer significant near-term pain because many doors to advanced AI computing power would effectively be shut.
Chinese companies would have little choice but to rely on their existing stock of restricted chips and domestic production. Supply through both channels is quite limited.
However, I do not think the Nvidia saga changes the long-term direction of US-China AI or technology competition. China’s push for semiconductor self-sufficiency has been under way for many years.
For Beijing, reducing reliance on foreign technology and building an indigenous Chinese technology stack has almost always been a priority – arguably as important as seeing Chinese AI labs dominate global benchmarks.
Before the Nvidia saga, Chinese AI companies preferred foreign chips because they were better. There was a degree of misalignment between the government’s priorities and what the companies wanted.
Now, with the saga and new restrictions, Chinese companies may have fewer fantasies about continued access to foreign chips and will more fully embrace domestic alternatives.
This will only accelerate the development of the domestic tech stack, because it will lead to more user feedback and kick off a positive feedback loop that helps them improve.
[embedded media]
What does Huang’s departure and comeback mean for global AI demand?
Huang is certainly irreplaceable and highly influential in the global AI sector. His comeback is good for Nvidia’s business and the global AI sector, but it does not resolve ongoing concerns over AI’s return on investment, circular financing, rising cost of capital or the changing political environment after the midterms.
One big variable is the new BIS remote-access rule.
If BIS enforces it very strictly, a lot of Chinese remote access to computing power could be cut off. We need to see whether those freed-up compute resources are easily reallocated.
[US President Donald Trump] has also made some bold claims on blocking US companies from building AI data centres overseas and imposing hefty taxes on firms that do so. This is contradictory to his diffusionist approach – but it’s Trump. If he does so, it will be really bad for US hyperscalers, as global diffusion is important if the US objective is to secure global leadership in AI before China catches up.
Compounded by the Democratic “blue wave”, we might see some slowdown in data centre buildouts and more market consolidation. However, that isn’t necessarily a bad thing – more disciplined, paced investment can be healthy for the industry in the long run.
If consolidation removes weaker players and weaker projects, it could also give US power infrastructure more time to catch up. Some estimates suggest that power constraints could become a serious bottleneck for US data-centre construction in late 2027 and 2028.
Another factor is US-China AI competition. Regardless of what happens in the US, the Chinese government remains firmly committed to developing AI.
Beijing appears to believe that AI is a transformative technology that can boost productivity, and it wants to diffuse AI across the economy and globally.
Competition between the US and China will give both countries strong incentives to sustain investment in AI.
[embedded media]
Does the new BIS rule change the nature of export controls?
I see the recent BIS rule less as a fundamental shift in the US approach and more as a very serious effort to close a loophole in existing export controls.
The US began limiting exports of advanced AI chips to China in October 2022, which focused on physical chips. However, until the latest BIS rule, remote access was considered legal.
That created an obvious policy gap. If Washington’s stated goal is to limit China’s access to advanced computing power, it does not make sense to limit physical chip exports while leaving the door wide open to remote access to those same chips.
My interpretation is that this contradiction was not necessarily the result of a calculated policy choice. It reflected incoherent policymaking in Washington and loopholes in the existing US export-control framework.
This was already a well-recognised loophole within Washington; Congress had been trying to close it since April 2024, when they first introduced the Remote Access Security Act.
So this whole Nvidia saga basically just added political urgency and accelerated that policy effort.
What does the new rule reveal about divisions in Washington?
There are two layers to the issue. One is potential corruption and knowing violations of export controls. There have been constant suspicions and speculation that improper business dealings or corruption may have been involved in the administration.
In my view, that is plausible, and we will find out more through the ongoing investigations.
The other layer is the debate over export controls themselves.
Export controls are difficult to calibrate. If they are too loose, they can give rivals the technology they need to improve their competitiveness and military capabilities, potentially threatening national security.
But if controls are too restrictive, they can hurt the revenue of domestic companies and potentially weaken their ability to invest in research and development. They can also incentivise rivals to double down on innovation and develop alternative systems.
Trump officials and tech CEOs have been divided on this export control debate regarding advanced chips.
On one side, you have the hawks advocating for tighter controls on national security grounds; on the other, you have Trump, Huang and [White House adviser] David Sacks advocating for diffusing the American tech stack globally to secure American technological leadership, market share and global influence.
They believe that maintaining global influence will deter rivals such as Huawei Technologies from developing highly competitive alternative systems.
The middle ground they reached was permitting the export of the H200, which was Nvidia’s third- or fourth-best chip. But the Nvidia saga, which involved remote access and chip diversion, complicated that debate.
The export controls did not work as intended. What I want to highlight is that this debate between control and diffusion is highly legitimate and not unique to Washington.
As China ascends in various tech sectors, the Chinese government is also releasing technology export controls, and we can see from policy documents that Beijing is wrestling with the same balancing act.
[embedded media]
Is the “small yard, high fence” expanding?
The yard is certainly getting bigger and the fence is getting higher. The problem is that the boundary is difficult to draw, because national security is a very broadly defined concept.
In export controls, I think the focus will gradually shift from restricting access to advanced chips – an area where the US has already done a great deal – to controls on semiconductor manufacturing equipment.
The argument is that if controls on equipment are looser than controls on the chips themselves, they will simply enable China to manufacture its own chips. That would undermine the purpose of the restrictions.
The US has already been implementing pretty strict equipment controls since 2022, though there are still loopholes in the framework.
The bill to watch very closely will be the Match Act, which would force US allies to align with US export controls, with a special focus on advanced lithography machines from [Dutch equipment maker] ASML.
That bill would have major consequences because it would not only restrict more tool exports, but also potentially suspend components and services for existing advanced lithography systems, which would have a very damaging impact on China’s existing production capacity of advanced chips.
There is also a parallel concern in the US regarding Chinese products and components in US communications networks, infrastructure and supply chains.
The [US Federal Communications Commission] has been spearheading quite a bit of restriction there, targeting a wide range of Chinese imports.
We’re talking about things like drones, robots and power inverters, and now there is discussion about potentially blocking optical transceivers.
The FCC’s concerns revolve around data security, cybersecurity and over-reliance on Chinese supply chains, which they believe pose a significant national security threat.
Just as China is pursuing self-sufficiency, the US is pursuing very similar goals in strategic sectors.
Of course, there is a disconnect between policy ambitions and practical reality for both sides, but the trend of strategic decoupling at this point is irreversible.
How effective have US technology controls been?
The impact of these controls has been uneven, as the control regime on advanced-chip exports has proved quite porous because of remote access and chip diversion.
But one point I want to emphasise: even though China has continued to gain access through these channels, the restrictions have raised costs for Chinese AI companies and supply remains limited.
As a result, we are seeing greater adoption of domestic chips. That is helping domestic products improve.
Compute constraints have also encouraged innovation in China in areas such as algorithms, model architecture, inference efficiency and compute-cluster management, because Chinese companies need to operate different types of chips within the same cluster and need to maximise utilisation of limited compute resources.
That progress will enhance the competitiveness of China’s technology stack.
However, controls on high-bandwidth memory (HBM) and semiconductor manufacturing equipment have created much greater challenges for China, because they directly affect China’s ability to expand onshore advanced chip manufacturing capacity.
Domestic HBM production is also constrained to a large extent by these tool restrictions. While these restrictions have certainly created fresh opportunities for domestic toolmakers – and Chinese toolmakers are indeed making progress in certain categories – many critical gaps remain.
I would caution against a common analogy between China’s semiconductor catch-up and its success in electric vehicles.
Advanced semiconductor manufacturing is perhaps the single most complex and globalised industrial process in the world, involving more than a thousand complex process steps and requiring hundreds of advanced tools to work reliably together.
The constraint isn’t just lithography, which always grabs the headlines; it spans a wide range of different tools, software and know-how. Foreign incumbents have spent decades accumulating this technology, know-how, IP and reliability track record.
So while I am confident in China’s ability to eventually make a breakthrough, I believe it will be a very lengthy and capital-intensive process.
[embedded media]
Can opposition from US allies weaken the Match Act?
The Dutch government and ASML have consistently opposed tighter controls on the export of lithography machines to China. Under US pressure, however, the Dutch government agreed to restrictions on ASML’s advanced immersion-lithography systems.
My view is that opposition from the Dutch government as well as from ASML is unlikely to be the deciding factor. These parties have limited leverage.
Ultimately, the outcome will depend on Washington’s own assessment of the controls and on China’s response.
What is the outlook on tech after the US midterm elections?
I am not an expert on US politics, but I can share my views.
The various export controls on China have had bipartisan support. It is not just the Democrats; there is support across both parties.
The main people slowing these controls were Trump and a small number of his officials, as well as Jensen Huang and his lobbying efforts, because they were not fully on board for a variety of reasons.
My reading of the midterms is that China is not the central issue for Democrats. Their priorities are more likely to be affordability and inflation, investigating potential corruption in the Trump administration, ending the Iran war and ending the Russia-Ukraine war.
After January, however, I think the single biggest variable to watch will be the outcome of the investigations into Nvidia and Huang. Trump’s personal intervention to reinstate Huang as CEO has already invigorated the hawks and Democrats.
If the investigations uncover corruption or questionable business dealings within the administration, or serious export-control violations by Nvidia or Huang, that would almost certainly inject fresh momentum into a more hawkish US technology policy towards China. We could expect even tighter controls.
Will scrutiny spread to AMD and other US chipmakers?
Broadly speaking, the Nvidia saga is likely to attract fresh scrutiny of American companies with ties to China. Those ties could be personal or commercial, and investigators may examine whether business dealings are questionable.
In the semiconductor sector, the key question is whether there has been any transfer of technology or products, including chips, in violation of US export controls. There may also be other business dealings that are considered sensitive or impermissible under US rules.
AMD is an obvious target for scrutiny. I am not sure that this is because of personal ties. A more likely reason is that AMD is the second choice for Chinese buyers seeking advanced AI chips.
I had a quick skim of the original short-seller report. I think it contains some errors. AMD’s revenue in China does not come exclusively from AI chips. The company also sells a substantial amount of CPU products there. Those errors raise questions about the report’s credibility.
I would also highlight that, shortly after China shut the door on Nvidia’s H200, AMD held a high-profile event involving its China business. It even advertised itself as “Advanced Mutual Development” at the event. AMD is clearly trying to capture some of the market share Nvidia has lost.
But that is not proof that AMD has done anything wrong. The Trump administration approved the export of some AMD chips to China.
Based on what I have heard from people on the ground, I have not heard of AMD chips being diverted. They are also not as desirable to Chinese buyers as Nvidia’s chips.
Where are China’s biggest vulnerabilities in AI and semiconductors?
Start with semiconductors. China can design chips, so chip design is not really the problem. It can also develop world-leading AI models, as we have already seen.
The constraint is advanced computing power, which is very important because data, algorithms and computing power are the three key elements of AI.
Now that the door to foreign chips is basically shut, hopes rest on domestic production. But I would describe the bottleneck as a whole-supply-chain problem for the advanced semiconductor stack.
China’s self-sufficiency across the entire stack – ranging from advanced tools and their critical components to advanced semiconductor materials, electronic design automation tools and packaging – still depends heavily on foreign technologies and suppliers.
As for the AI stack, China has done a very good job in algorithmic innovation, inference efficiency and cost management.
China also claims to have a major advantage in data because it has a huge manufacturing base and many industries operating domestically.
That creates data availability. But Chinese industrial data is often fragmented and not standardised, so it is not necessarily ready for model training.
That is why the Chinese government is orchestrating a top-down effort to collect and organise high-quality data sets. If that effort succeeds, China could have a considerable advantage in this area.
Monetisation is definitely important. Data is expensive, and AI compute, safety testing and experimental research are expensive.
Given the current technology sell-off and the persistent monetisation challenges facing Chinese AI models, the question of how these companies will generate returns is an important one.
How are Chinese AI companies monetising their technology?
Monetisation is different for hyperscalers such as ByteDance and [South China Morning Post owner] Alibaba, compared with independent AI labs. For independent labs, their main revenue sources are local deployment services or application programming interfaces (APIs).
Looking at the financials of listed labs, they are deriving an increasing proportion of their revenue from overseas. The question is whether that overseas revenue is sustainable given the new controls.
Even with overseas sales, their API revenue remains very small compared with the US frontier labs, raising the question of whether they can generate enough revenue to recover their costs.
For the hyperscalers like ByteDance, it’s a two-part story.
First, they incorporate AI into internal business to improve efficiency and generate more revenue, including through e-commerce and advertising.
Second, companies like ByteDance and Alibaba pursue a full-stack strategy offering cloud services, leveraging their compute resources to provide models-as-a-service.
Alibaba’s earnings have already shown that the margins from providing its own models and third-party models are very similar. As long as a company has computing resources, it can monetise them.
The other area is stand-alone AI applications. There is still limited evidence that these applications can generate sufficient revenue.
That is due to several factors, including consumers’ low willingness to pay in China and intense competition among companies, with subsidies and price competition.
One bright spot is video generation models, particularly from ByteDance, which benefit from vertical integration across content distribution and video models.
They have done well, though a major downstream application of video models – microdramas – is becoming extremely cutthroat and crowded. So there are still questions about how sustainable that growth is going forward.
Lastly, revenue could come from AI hardware. China has a very strong manufacturing supply chain and cost advantage.
It can produce hardware at scale and add AI capabilities to it. There could be decent opportunities if China can produce attractive AI hardware.
Just like in other manufacturing sectors, even if the domestic market doesn’t generate high margins, companies can export overseas where there is plenty of demand. That’s definitely a space to watch.
[embedded media]
Which country is better positioned to export its AI stack globally?
The practical problem is that China does not yet have a complete AI stack that it can export at scale because it lacks advanced chips.
Even if Chinese models are adopted, they often run on US chips, including in [Belt and Road Initiative] countries. That is still a significant disadvantage.
China’s limited onshore production of advanced chips will remain a substantial bottleneck to diffusing its AI stack in the near term, and that likely won’t be resolved in the next two to three years.
Furthermore, with the crackdown on model distillation and remote access, there are questions about how fast Chinese models can continue advancing.
Chinese companies can still generate revenue by providing local deployment services for smaller models running on existing hardware, but in the near term, as long as the US continues to push global diffusion, the US is likely to hold the upper hand.
Can China eventually replace advanced US chips?
All these challenges and workarounds come down to the same fundamental issue: chip manufacturing.
Even if you use a supernode architecture to compensate for lower single-chip performance by networking many chips together, you still need a massive volume of chips, so it again comes down to chip manufacturing.
You can design these architectures on paper and in theory, but the real test is whether you can mass-produce them in volume using reliable equipment in a profitable manner.
Profitability is secondary here – the core question is mass production, which brings us right back to China’s lag in advanced semiconductor equipment.
Catching up in equipment isn’t easy. Beyond technology and know-how, you face strict IP walls, and even after building a tool, it takes at least two to three years of reliability testing to achieve the desired yields.
So there are no quick short cuts in moving forward. However, because of these constraints, China will definitely double down on exploring all alternative pathways, and by concentrating a whole-of-nation effort, it may eventually find breakthroughs.
Where could China make the biggest breakthroughs in semiconductor equipment?
In equipment, China may have a better chance of making progress in areas where demand is greatest.
For instance, etching, deposition and hybrid bonding tools. There are still substantial gaps, but these tools are needed for multiple critical applications, so China may be able to mobilise more resources and effort. There are also some good Chinese companies in these areas.
Breakthroughs in advanced lithography, particularly extreme ultraviolet lithography, will be extremely difficult. Inspection and metrology equipment will also be very tough nuts to crack.
Does China have an energy advantage in AI?
I think China’s energy advantage in AI is somewhat overstated.
Energy is very important. China’s power grid is the world’s largest and one of its most advanced, and it continues to add generation capacity.
But China’s electricity advantage is not so much about the cost of electricity; it is about the availability of energy.
[embedded media]
Another point that is often misunderstood is the share of electricity in data-centre costs.
Electricity accounts for about one-quarter of the annual operating expenditure of a US data centre.
But if you factor in both operating expenditure and capital expenditure, electricity accounts for only about 7 per cent of the all-in annual cost of a US data centre.
So even if China has an overwhelming advantage in electricity costs, that may not matter as much as people think.
The bulk of the all-in cost – around 60 per cent – is the servers, where China does not have an advantage.
That said, power availability will matter a great deal if the US hits grid bottlenecks.
We could end up with a very interesting dynamic in the coming years: China builds plenty of data centres with abundant power, waiting on advanced chips, while the US has plenty of advanced chips, waiting on power.
How effective are China’s rare earth countermeasures?
Trump’s claim [of catching up with China in rare earth in 10 months] is highly exaggerated.
Rare earths have genuinely been China’s trump card, and their potency will last well into the foreseeable future.
Even though we are seeing concerted efforts by the US and its allies to build alternative supply chains, that will be a very lengthy process.
Japan is probably the best example. Even after about 15 years of effort, Japan – a technologically advanced country – has only reduced its dependence on China for rare earth imports from around 90 per cent in 2010 to about 65 to 70 per cent today.
This shows that while China’s leverage may diminish gradually over time, substantially eliminating it is a multi-decade endeavour.
A realistic assessment for the US is that it could achieve high self-sufficiency in rare earths for the defence sector within two to three years, since defence volumes are relatively small.
However, it is likely to take 10 years or more for the US to reduce its dependence on Chinese rare earths across broader civilian sectors.
That matters enormously because we are talking about critical materials used across countless civilian applications, including the semiconductor industry itself.
Unlike US export controls on chips and equipment, China’s dominance in rare earths can have an immediate effect on global supply chains. China has been approving export licences selectively and incrementally, using that process to extend its leverage.
So far, that approach appears to have worked, as we have seen in the back-and-forth in bilateral relations.

title_en: China pushes brain-computer interface breakthroughs as Neuralink advances towards market
content_en:
Beijing bets on standards and wider clinical applications in a bid to pull ahead in the emerging industry.
A brain-computer interface system is showcased in Beijing on July 26. Photo: Getty Images
Chinese firms are racing to claim brain-computer interface (BCI) breakthroughs as Elon Musk’s Neuralink advances towards commercialisation, with Beijing seeking to leapfrog the US by setting standards and expanding real-world applications in what it sees as a strategic industry.
Neuralink said on Wednesday it would launch a late-stage trial to evaluate the safety and effectiveness of its implantable BCI device for adults living with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), allowing them to control digital devices using their thoughts.
The study would be the first pivotal trial for an implantable BCI device in the US, with the company calling it “an important step” towards bringing the technology to market.
According to the US Food and Drug Administration website, “pivotal” studies followed “exploratory” trials that assessed a product’s feasibility and were designed to gather evidence needed for pre-market approval.
Neuralink said its ongoing early-stage studies across the US, Canada and the United Kingdom had enrolled more than 30 participants who had accumulated thousands of hours of real-world use.
Earlier this week, the Fremont, California-based company showcased a participant with quadriplegia – caused by a spinal cord injury – playing the blockbuster video game Grand Theft Auto VI using only his mind instead of a physical controller.
China has been accelerating efforts to compete with Neuralink in BCI technology, which Beijing has identified as one of six “industries of the future” in its latest five-year plan.
Hangzhou-based Kingstronics, a start-up jointly backed by Zhejiang University and the local government, said on Wednesday that it had achieved a breakthrough in using BCI to treat depression.
In an early clinical trial for its DeepAxtiv system, five of the six participants achieved remission, a rate of 83 per cent, the company said. The team had yet to publish peer-reviewed research on the results.
The China Academy of Information and Communications Technology, a think tank under the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, said in a report published earlier this week that China, the US and Europe were all “actively vying for influence” in BCI technology, and that the global industry landscape was facing a “reshuffle”.
While the US relied on venture capital to maintain its edge in foundational and frontier technology breakthroughs, China could gain an advantage by leaning on its manufacturing supply chain and broader clinical use cases, according to the think tank.
Chinese authorities are also stepping up efforts to shape standards for the emerging sector. The ministry on Wednesday established a new working group under its BCI standardisation technical committee to help advance real-world applications.
By Xinmei Shen

title_en: Alibaba sells US$482 million in ZTO Express shares as AI focus sharpens
content_en:
The second sell-off in two months lowers Alibaba’s stake in the logistics giant to 2.9 per cent.
A staff member sorts parcels at a ZTO Express location in Ningxia Hui autonomous region
on November 9. Photo: Xinhua
Alibaba Group Holding has sharply reduced its stake in Chinese logistics giant ZTO Express, raising roughly US$482 million in its second major sell-off of the courier’s shares in two months.
Alibaba and its three affiliates – Alibaba ZT Investment Limited, New Retail Strategic Opportunities Investments 2 Limited and Cainiao Smart Logistics Investment Limited – offloaded a combined 25 million Class A ordinary shares on Tuesday, according to a filing to the US Securities and Exchange Commission on Wednesday.
The sell-off brings Alibaba’s beneficial ownership in ZTO Express down to 2.9 per cent from 6.1 per cent, with around 21.9 million shares left. It also ends its obligation to publicly disclose future changes to its ZTO position, according to the company.
The stake was sold in the form of American Depositary Shares at US$19.28 each, amounting to around US$482 million.
While Alibaba did not officially specify a reason for the divestment, the retreat comes amid the tech giant’s broader push to shed noncore equity holdings and focus capital on its core e-commerce and artificial intelligence businesses.
In 2025, the company committed to investing at least 380 billion yuan (US$57.02 billion) over three years into cloud and AI infrastructure, in China’s largest-ever computing project financed by a single private business.
[embedded media]
The latest sale follows a previous round of divestment in September, when Alibaba sold 25 million shares in ZTO, raising around US$500 million. The two transactions have generated nearly US$1 billion in cash for the Hangzhou-based company.
ZTO is not the only logistics company that Alibaba has sought to streamline in its portfolio of China’s major express delivery operators over the past few months.
In September, Alibaba offloaded 45.8 million shares of SF Intra-city, a spin-off of SF Express, fully exiting from the on-demand delivery firm and raising roughly HK$392 million (US$50 million).
The company also trimmed its stake in YTO Express – another major logistics firm – from a peak level of 22.5 per cent in 2020 to roughly 15 per cent in June.
Still, the e-commerce giant maintains deep partnerships with the logistics companies despite scaling back at the equity level.
It announced it had reached a deal with SF Express in September, with the two companies exploring collaboration in areas including e-commerce fulfilment, cross-border logistics, intelligent supply chains and AI applications.
Alibaba owns the South China Morning Post.

title_en: Chinese AI chips to capture 88% of home market by 2028, UBS says, as Nvidia woes mount
content_en:
Over the next one to two years, a chipmaker’s ability to secure manufacturing capacity and key components will be its primary competitive edge.
Beijing is doubling down on tech self-reliance amid heightened scrutiny over US chip exports following the recent Nvidia saga. Photo: Shutterstock Images
China’s annual domestic artificial intelligence accelerator shipments are set to jump nearly sixfold between 2025 and 2030 to more than 10 million units, with Cambricon Technologies and Biren Technology emerging as front runners, according to UBS.
This comes as Beijing doubles down on technological self-reliance amid heightened scrutiny over US chip exports following the recent Nvidia saga.
Shipments of locally made AI processors – rising from 1.7 million units in 2025 – would propel Chinese suppliers’ share of their home market to 83 per cent in 2027 and 88 per cent in 2028, Jimmy Yu, head of China technology at UBS Securities, said in a research note published on Tuesday.
That would represent a gain of more than 40 percentage points from 2025 levels, at the expense of overseas incumbents.
“Demand for China’s graphics processing units [GPUs] and AI accelerators is surging, driven by rising domestic AI infrastructure buildout and capital expenditure, the pursuit of self-reliance and booming demand for agentic and other AI applications,” Yu wrote.
AI accelerators, which include GPUs, are used for training and running AI models. UBS noted that growth was also being underpinned by an improving local supply chain and rising demand for inference – the process of running trained models to generate outputs.
The Cambricon booth at the World Artificial Intelligence Conference in Shanghai, July 9, 2021. Photo: VCG via Getty Images
However, a shortage in high-bandwidth memory (HBM) – a component that enables AI processors to access large volumes of data quickly – alongside limited advanced chipmaking capacity – was expected to constrain shipments this year and next.
“While investors tend to focus on demand, we believe supply-chain constraints will be equally, if not more, important,” the report said.
Factoring in hurdles, UBS projected domestic GPU shipments would reach about 3.7 million units in 2027 and 5.5 million in 2028, falling 20 to 30 per cent short of projected demand. It expected growth to accelerate from 2028 as domestic supply expanded.
Over the next one to two years, a chipmaker’s ability to secure manufacturing capacity and key components would be its primary competitive edge, followed by partnerships with major cloud service providers (CSPs) and AI model developers, the report said.
“Based on our scoring framework, we believe Cambricon is better positioned than other listed names, given its scale, superior accelerator performance and close relationship with the largest CSP customer in China,” Yu wrote.
“We also see Biren [Technology]’s supply-chain relationship as a key differentiating factor relative to smaller domestic peers,” he added.
The domestic buildout unfolds amid tightening US export controls and recent leadership turmoil at Nvidia. On November 16, Washington unveiled new rules restricting Chinese access to advanced American chips via overseas data centres.
Days earlier, co-founder Jensen Huang had stepped down as CEO of the world’s most valuable AI chipmaker following reports of an alleged extramarital affair with a Chinese businesswoman formerly employed at Megaspeed, which was under US investigation for potential export control breaches.
Huang was reinstated as CEO on Monday.
The new US regulations require licences for certain exports, re-exports and transfers of advanced chips and servers to data centres providing substantial computing power to companies headquartered in China or other restricted destinations, or those whose ultimate parent companies are based there.
US President Donald Trump said on Friday that he wanted only older chips sold to China, adding that his administration was discussing an agreement with Beijing, without providing further details.
“A competitive domestic GPU ecosystem could reduce China’s dependence on foreign compute infrastructure while enabling faster and broader AI adoption across Chinese enterprises,” UBS said.
Additional reporting by Ann Cao
By Minxiao Chang

title_en: UN experts demand Vietnam explain ‘abduction’ of activists from Cambodia
content_en:
Critics say Vietnam’s security apparatus stretches abroad, with wanted dissidents previously abducted in Thailand and Germany.
People ride a moped past the National Assembly building in Hanoi in 2021. Vietnam permits little to no dissent within its borders. Photo: AP
Vietnam must explain how three pro-democracy activists ended up in detention facing terrorism charges after being allegedly abducted from neighbouring Cambodia, United Nations experts said on Thursday.
Vietnam permits little to no dissent within its borders and critics say its security apparatus stretches abroad, with wanted dissidents previously abducted in Thailand and Germany.
The authorities in Hanoi confirmed in September they had arrested three men – an Australian, a Norwegian and a Vietnamese national – on charges of terrorism and forging documents.
“We urge Vietnam to disclose the circumstances and legal basis of the arrests,” said the experts, who are mandated by the UN Human Rights Council but do not speak on behalf of the United Nations itself.
Nguyen Duc Thuan, a Norwegian passport holder, has been detained by Vietnamese authorities. Photo: Viet Tan / dpa
They said Cambodia had a duty to investigate, while Vietnam must cooperate and detail “any involvement of its officials in the alleged abductions, transfers and enforced disappearances”.
“We are alarmed by these alleged transboundary abductions, which violate international human rights law,” they said.
Rights group Viet Tan raised the alarm in late September, saying two of its members had been abducted by Vietnamese authorities from across the border in Cambodia, forcibly brought to Vietnam and detained on “fabricated” terrorism charges.
Nguyen Duc Thuan, a Norwegian citizen, and Australian national Tran Hiep, also known as Ho Pham Hiep Huy, had been reported missing since September 18.
Vietnam’s public security ministry later confirmed the pair had been arrested along with a Vietnamese man, Thai Cong Truong Son, who was not identified by Viet Tan as one of its members.
The terrorism charge carries a maximum sentence of 15 years in jail.
More than 160 political prisoners are detained in Vietnam, according to the NGO Human Rights Watch.
By Agence France-Presse

title_en: Japan plans new long-range anti-ship missile to bolster naval build-up
content_en:
Analysts argue this may complicate China’s wartime planning by allowing a wider range of Japanese ships to carry the missiles.
Photo taken on November 10 shows Harpoon anti-ship missiles (L) and a Phalanx rapid-fire 20-millimeter gun system (R) equipped on the Sendai destroyer docked at a port in Maizuru, Kyoto prefecture. Photo: Kyodo
Tokyo is planning to introduce a new long-range anti-ship missile that could be launched from a broader range of vessels, according to Japanese media reports, potentially complicating Chinese military planning in a conflict.
The proposed capability could allow Japan to equip vessels that traditionally do not carry anti-ship missiles, according to defence experts.
The country is also looking to deploy a persistent surveillance system in medium Earth orbit to improve its ability to detect and track enemy warships, part of a broader effort to strengthen its counterstrike capabilities.
Both proposals were outlined in draft guidelines for Japan’s next five-year defence build-up programme, Kyodo News reported on Wednesday. The programme is one of three key national security documents the government plans to revise by the end of the year.
The Japanese government will reportedly examine whether the new missile could be operated from box-shaped launchers that resemble shipping containers and can be placed aboard various types of naval vessels.
Tokyo’s push comes amid increasingly strained relations with Beijing, particularly over the issue of Taiwan, and growing concerns in Japan over the expanding People’s Liberation Army.
[embedded media]
China has the world’s biggest navy by number of ships and continues to expand and modernise its fleet. Its shipyards accounted for more than 43 per cent of global naval production tonnage in 2024 and 2025, more than twice the US share, according to a recent survey.
Beijing has repeatedly criticised Tokyo’s planned security revisions, with both the foreign and defence ministries of China accusing Japan of accelerating its “remilitarisation” and challenging the post-war international order.
While the exact type of missile Tokyo envisages remains unclear, documents reviewed by the South China Morning Post show that Japan’s defence procurement agency had already begun exploring acquisition options over three months ago.
In a notice dated August 12, the agency invited Japanese companies with experience designing or manufacturing guided-missile systems to express interest in providing information and discussing technical options for a new naval anti-ship missile and containerised launcher.
Defence expert Yoshihiro Inaba, the Japan correspondent for the Naval News website, said the Japan Maritime Self-Defence Force (SDF) had long been interested in containerised missile launch systems, but the latest reports suggested the initiative was moving beyond the research stage.
“Based on the latest media reports, this research effort is now set to transition into the actual development phase of the weapon system,” Inaba said.
Among the vessels that could carry the new missile, Inaba said, were the Maritime SDF’s offshore patrol vessels, transport ships and replenishment ships.
[embedded media]
“In the event of a potential conflict with China, the Chinese military would have to account for the possibility that virtually any Japan Maritime SDF vessel could be armed with long-range missiles,” Inaba said.
“The apparent intention is to complicate China’s operational planning and military calculations.”
Japan is already acquiring a ship-launched variant of its upgraded Type 12 anti-ship missile for use aboard destroyers, with the defence ministry allocating 35.7 billion yen (US$224 million) for its acquisition in the current financial year.
Inaba suggested that the proposed container-launched missile could draw on technology from an anti-ship missile for island defence that Kawasaki Heavy Industries has been researching since 2023.
Designed to strike enemy warships and landing forces, the Kawasaki missile prototype underwent its first launch test last year.
Beyond the missile proposal, the draft defence build-up guidelines call for a satellite surveillance system capable of continuously monitoring vast areas from medium Earth orbit, according to Kyodo.
The system could complement Japan’s planned low Earth orbit satellite constellation, as satellites in higher orbits are generally able to observe larger areas.
In its Space Domain Defence Guidelines, released in July last year, the Japanese defence ministry said it would consider developing observation satellites in higher orbits.
However, that document did not specifically identify medium Earth orbit as a potential zone for surveillance operations.
[embedded media]
The draft guidelines also called for the acquisition of medium-sized uncrewed surface vessels for search-and-rescue missions and missile launches, as well as satellites to protect Japanese spacecraft against potential attacks by Chinese and Russian satellites, Kyodo reported.
The government is also seeking to promote domestic production of defence equipment across all sectors to enable rapid increases in manufacturing in the event of a conflict.
The guidelines also recommend reviewing the organisation and troop numbers of the Ground Self-Defence Force amid recruitment difficulties and a declining birth rate.
The measures are part of a broader overhaul of Japan’s three main strategic security documents, which also include the country’s National Security and National Defence strategies. The revised documents are expected to be released next month.
How much of the proposed military build-up will ultimately be implemented remains unclear. Fiscal pressures appear to be prompting Tokyo to consider a smaller defence budget than the 70 trillion to 80 trillion yen proposed by the defence ministry, but still well above the 43 trillion yen allocated under the current five-year programme.
By Gabriel Dominguez

title_en: Russian court jails Colombian fighter for 20 years over Ukraine war role
content_en:
Colombians are sought in fighting around the world due to their extensive experience of armed combat.
Ukrainian soldiers gather beside a ground drone beneath anti-drone netting on a road between Kramatorsk and Druzhkivka in Ukraine’s Donetsk region on Tuesday. Photo Ukraine’s 93rd Mechanised Brigade / AP
A court in Ukraine’s Moscow-annexed Donetsk region jailed a Colombian for 20 years, saying he was a mercenary fighting for Kyiv, Russia said on Thursday.
The Russian Prosecutor General’s Office said the court “has handed down a verdict in the criminal case against 33-year-old Colombian national Cristian Morales Mendoza”, adding he was “a mercenary in an armed conflict”.
Both Moscow and Kyiv have recruited thousands of foreigners in their armies since Russia launched its offensive in Ukraine nearly five years ago.
Last month, the South American country’s foreign ministry reported that over 250 Colombians had died and almost 1,000 had disappeared while fighting in the war.
Colombian demonstrators take part in a protest in support of Ukraine in front of the Russian Embassy in Bogota on February 26, 2022. Photo: AFP
In Ukraine, 162 Colombians have died and 666 have disappeared, while on the Russian side, 94 have perished and 297 are missing, according to the ministry.
The United Nations estimates that at least 10,000 Colombian mercenaries are fighting abroad, lured by often false promises of high salaries and security, and in many cases battling under inhumane conditions.
At least 7,000 of them have joined the Russia-Ukraine war, government data published in May showed.
Colombians are sought in fighting around the world due to their extensive experience of armed combat, and thousands have been pulled into the conflict.
Since 2022, several foreign nationals have been convicted and imprisoned by the Russian justice system for fighting as mercenaries on behalf of Ukraine.
Maritime spread
Russia ⁠attacked two foreign ‌civilian ships carrying more than ⁠100,000 tonnes of ‌grain overnight ‌near Ukraine’s Black ⁠Sea ⁠port ‌of Odesa, ‌Ukraine’s ‌Prime ‌Minister Sergiy ⁠Koretskyi said on ⁠Thursday.
The Kremlin on Thursday accused Ukraine of ⁠trying to spread the war ⁠to the Mediterranean and Baltic seas, a move it called very dangerous.
US President Donald Trump and Nato chief Mark Rutte said in a joint statement on Wednesday after a meeting in Florida ‌that Russia should avoid actions that expand the war.
Their intervention appeared to be a warning to Moscow to think twice about how it retaliated against Ukraine over recent attacks Kyiv has launched on Russian interests far from the conflict zone.
Smoke rises over Kyiv on Thursday after overnight Russian missile strikes. Photo: Reuters
Ukraine sank a Russian naval corvette in a ⁠Libyan port using maritime drones on Sunday, a day after it carried out a drone strike ‌on a Russian military-linked cargo ship in the Gulf of Finland.
Responding to the joint US-Nato statement, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said that nobody ‌wanted the conflict to expand, but he said Ukraine, not Russia, was the ⁠one trying to ⁠widen the area of conflict.
“As regards the escalation of the conflict in Ukraine, this appears to refer to ‌attempts by the Kyiv regime to expand the geographical scope of this conflict. We are witnessing terrorist activity by the Kyiv ‌regime ‌in the Mediterranean and the Baltic,” Peskov told reporters on a conference call.
“This cannot ‌fail to cause concern amongst coastal states, and most likely within [Nato] as a ⁠whole. Of course, nobody would want the conflict to spread geographically, ⁠and these are potentially very dangerous actions on the part of the Kyiv regime.”
Libyan authorities condemned Ukraine’s actions, as did Italy which told Kyiv it ‌was wrong to attack ‌Russian ships in Libyan waters and warned it not to spread the war to new areas.
Norway, a strong supporter of Kyiv, also urged it to exercise caution in any Baltic Sea operations and stressed the need to maintain stability in areas close to it.

title_display: Russian court jails Colombian fighter for 20 years over Ukraine war role
content_display:
Colombians are sought in fighting around the world due to their extensive experience of armed combat.
Ukrainian soldiers gather beside a ground drone beneath anti-drone netting on a road between Kramatorsk and Druzhkivka in Ukraine’s Donetsk region on Tuesday. Photo Ukraine’s 93rd Mechanised Brigade / AP
A court in Ukraine’s Moscow-annexed Donetsk region jailed a Colombian for 20 years, saying he was a mercenary fighting for Kyiv, Russia said on Thursday.
The Russian Prosecutor General’s Office said the court “has handed down a verdict in the criminal case against 33-year-old Colombian national Cristian Morales Mendoza”, adding he was “a mercenary in an armed conflict”.
Both Moscow and Kyiv have recruited thousands of foreigners in their armies since Russia launched its offensive in Ukraine nearly five years ago.
Last month, the South American country’s foreign ministry reported that over 250 Colombians had died and almost 1,000 had disappeared while fighting in the war.
Colombian demonstrators take part in a protest in support of Ukraine in front of the Russian Embassy in Bogota on February 26, 2022. Photo: AFP
In Ukraine, 162 Colombians have died and 666 have disappeared, while on the Russian side, 94 have perished and 297 are missing, according to the ministry.
The United Nations estimates that at least 10,000 Colombian mercenaries are fighting abroad, lured by often false promises of high salaries and security, and in many cases battling under inhumane conditions.
At least 7,000 of them have joined the Russia-Ukraine war, government data published in May showed.
Colombians are sought in fighting around the world due to their extensive experience of armed combat, and thousands have been pulled into the conflict.
Since 2022, several foreign nationals have been convicted and imprisoned by the Russian justice system for fighting as mercenaries on behalf of Ukraine.
Maritime spread
Russia ⁠attacked two foreign ‌civilian ships carrying more than ⁠100,000 tonnes of ‌grain overnight ‌near Ukraine’s Black ⁠Sea ⁠port ‌of Odesa, ‌Ukraine’s ‌Prime ‌Minister Sergiy ⁠Koretskyi said on ⁠Thursday.
The Kremlin on Thursday accused Ukraine of ⁠trying to spread the war ⁠to the Mediterranean and Baltic seas, a move it called very dangerous.
US President Donald Trump and Nato chief Mark Rutte said in a joint statement on Wednesday after a meeting in Florida ‌that Russia should avoid actions that expand the war.
Their intervention appeared to be a warning to Moscow to think twice about how it retaliated against Ukraine over recent attacks Kyiv has launched on Russian interests far from the conflict zone.
Smoke rises over Kyiv on Thursday after overnight Russian missile strikes. Photo: Reuters
Ukraine sank a Russian naval corvette in a ⁠Libyan port using maritime drones on Sunday, a day after it carried out a drone strike ‌on a Russian military-linked cargo ship in the Gulf of Finland.
Responding to the joint US-Nato statement, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said that nobody ‌wanted the conflict to expand, but he said Ukraine, not Russia, was the ⁠one trying to ⁠widen the area of conflict.

title_en: Will Solomon Islands’ Australia treaty prompt China to rethink its Pacific strategy?
content_en:
Honiara’s pivot reflects domestic pragmatism, not a regional trend, analysts say, but exposes fragile trust between Beijing and Canberra.
Solomon Islands Prime Minister Matthew Wale holds up a copy of the security treaty his country and Australia signed at Parliament House in Canberra on Wednesday, as Prime Minister Anthony Albanese looks on. Photo: AAP Image via AP
The Solomon Islands’ decision to replace its 2022 security pact with China with a sweeping new Australian treaty may push Beijing to rethink its Pacific playbook, observers say.
While some analysts said Honiara’s pivot reflected hard-nosed domestic pragmatism rather than a regional rush to shut out Beijing, others warned that Beijing must be wary of Canberra using the pact as a foothold to extend exclusive demands from security into economic and development ties.
The assessment was made as the Pacific neighbours signed a treaty on Wednesday in which the Solomon Islands agreed that its territory would not be used to establish foreign military bases and that it would commit to keeping its sensitive infrastructure – including airports and ports – “free from militarisation, any form of foreign interference or unauthorised access”.
The Solomon Islands has affirmed Australia as its main security partner and said it would look to members of the Pacific Islands Forum – of which China is not a member – for future security cooperation needs.
Beijing sought to play down developments, with foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun affirming that China’s ties with the Solomon Islands were based on “mutual respect and equality”, with “no element of geopolitical rivalry”. He added that cooperation “should not target any third party”.
Wednesday’s deal is widely seen as a major setback to China’s strategic position in the South Pacific, a region that has become a key arena for geopolitical rivalry as Beijing expands its economic and diplomatic footprint into Canberra’s traditional sphere of influence.
That has included billions of dollars of investment in infrastructure, from stadiums to hospitals, while Beijing has steadily expanded its security reach through bilateral law-enforcement cooperation – most notably in Honiara, where Chinese police have been training and advising local officers on rotating deployments since 2022.
Solomon Islands Prime Minister Matthew Wale during a signing ceremony with Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese in Canberra on Wednesday. Photo: AFP
Prime Minister Matthew Wale, who met his Australian counterpart Anthony Albanese in Canberra on Wednesday, declined to comment on the status of the security pact with China, citing nondisclosure clauses.
The Sydney Morning Herald reported on Tuesday, citing unnamed Solomon Islands sources, that Honiara had notified Beijing it would not renew the five-year agreement when it expires in April.
Chen Hong, director of the Australian Studies Centre at East China Normal University in Shanghai, said that if the Solomon Islands did not renew the pact, that would “undoubtedly weigh on bilateral ties, especially strategic trust”.
“However, security cooperation is only one component of the relationship, and the fate of a single agreement cannot be equated with the broader trajectory of bilateral ties,” he said.
But he warned that the real risk to Beijing was that the change could become a starting point for Australia to wade deeper into the Solomon Islands’ foreign policymaking by “extending exclusive demands from security into economic and development areas”.
“In that case, the impact on China-Solomon Islands relations would go far beyond a single security pact,” Chen said.
Edward Chan Sing-yue, a postdoctoral fellow in China studies at the Australian National University, said Beijing’s main concern was avoiding the “geopoliticisation or over-securitisation” of its engagement with the Global South.
Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi shakes hands with his Solomon Islands counterpart, Rick Houenipwela, during talks in Beijing in July. Photo: Xinhua
“Beijing needs to think further about how to deepen mutual trust and refine how it works with Pacific island states, including the Solomon Islands, both to maximise mutual interests and to gain a better grasp of local needs and cultures,” he said.
Relations with Honiara, which were only established in 2019, were still relatively new, Chan noted.
“Bilateral ties are still in an exploratory stage, having only been established three years before the security pact was signed,” he said. “Rather than souring the relationship, this episode could prompt Beijing to rethink its partnership model with Honiara – as well as its broader ties with other Pacific island states.”
Under the new deal, Australia will provide “substantial support” for the Solomon Islands’ free education policy, increase investment in sustainable infrastructure, and “strengthen people-to-people connections through culture, sport and the arts”.
Canberra will also expand work opportunities and improve visa arrangements for Solomon Islanders in Australia, according to a joint statement by the two prime ministers.
Wednesday’s treaty is seen as a major step in cementing Canberra’s regional clout, part of a broader push in which Australia has secured security and defence partnerships with Pacific island states, including Papua New Guinea, Vanuatu and Fiji, fuelling speculation that more nations could follow suit.
[embedded media]
Sandra Tarte, associate professor in the school of law and social sciences at the University of the South Pacific in Suva, Fiji, said the financial and defence incentives Australia provided were significant and “difficult to turn down”.
“Other countries already have treaties with Australia or are considering them,” she said.
But, she added, it would be naive to assume these countries would rule out ties with China.
“Most Pacific island countries will continue to court China’s economic assistance as well as commercial ties,” Tarte said. “Political changes within these countries may also lead to future diplomatic realignment towards China.”
Beijing would continue to view the South Pacific through a strategic lens, she added.
“While there may be setbacks, China is now an integral part of the region’s security and economic order. This role will only continue to grow in the future.”
Chan noted that Wednesday’s treaty was partly a result of Canberra’s years-long investment in regional ties – through aid, security and people-to-people links – as well as Honiara’s domestic political recalibration following Wale’s rise to power earlier this year. The new prime minister has long been critical of the 2022 security pact with China.
Solomon Islands Prime Minister Matthew Wale inspects the guard of honour during a welcome ceremony at Parliament House in Canberra on Wednesday. Photo: EPA
“Pacific island governments are generally reluctant to be drawn into geopolitics or great-power rivalry, and care more about whose terms best serve their national development interests,” Chan said.
“Rather than worrying about a domino effect, it is more accurate to say that Pacific island nations are more proactively leveraging the space created by great-power competition to secure the most advantageous terms of cooperation for themselves.”
Still, observers said, the Solomon Islands’ switch exposed the fragile trust between Beijing and Canberra, even as the two sides were now working to stabilise their broader trade relationship.
“Both governments seem to have realised that the political space for discussing South Pacific issues is narrowing,” Chan said, noting that neither government mentioned the region in its official statement about last week’s meeting between Albanese and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen.
Chan noted a mutual wish on the part of Beijing and Canberra to shield their warming economic ties from the dispute. “Both sides now tend to set aside their differences over the South Pacific to keep them from spilling over into the wider relationship.”
By Laura Zhou

title_en: Malaysian police close in on mastermind in air force drug-smuggling case
content_en:
Home Minister Saifuddin Nasution Ismail has promised more arrests ‘in the coming days’ and that those caught ‘will not escape’.
Malaysian army personnel load supplies into a plane at the Subang Air Force Base in 2017. Drugs were discovered during an inspection at the facility. Photo: AP
Malaysian police are closing in on the suspected ringleader of a drug-trafficking syndicate accused of using military assets to smuggle three tonnes of methamphetamine over more than two years, with a minister saying further arrests are expected “in the coming days”.
Seven air force personnel were among 13 people arrested after police discovered nearly 97kg of methamphetamine on November 17 during a routine luggage check at the Subang Air Force Base, about 30km from the capital city of Kuala Lumpur.
Police announced two days later that a drug-trafficking syndicate had been using the air force’s facilities to smuggle drugs to Sabah state on Malaysian Borneo before distributing them to international markets.
Home Minister Saifuddin Nasution Ismail on Thursday said police had already identified the mastermind behind the syndicate, along with several other “names or those that we think have positions in society”.
“I give my guarantee that whoever is to be arrested in the coming days will not escape, regardless of their rank, regardless of their position,” Saifuddin told parliament during Question Time.
Malaysia’s Home Minister Saifuddin Nasution Ismail (left) at the Asean Ministerial Meeting on Transnational Crime in Metro Manila, the Philippines, on October 21. Photo: EPA
The minister said the November 17 haul, valued at 4.83 million ringgit (US$1.8 million), was just a fraction of the volume that was moved by the syndicate in multiple tranches as far back as August 2024.
The syndicate had carried out 14 transactions out of the air force’s base on Labuan Island, off Sabah’s west coast, involving 1.2 tonnes of methamphetamine worth 63 million ringgit, Saifuddin said.
Another 1.8 tonnes of the drug, valued at 93 million ringgit, was transported to the air force’s base in Tawau on Sabah’s east coast, which shares a land border with Indonesia’s Kalimantan province and serves as a regular landing point for boats headed to and from the south of the Philippines.
The amount of methamphetamine trafficked by the syndicate through the air force’s facilities would have been enough to meet the demand of about 15 million users, the minister added.
“Early investigations have established the involvement of individuals who had access and relations with military personnel and flight operations,” Saifuddin said.
“We believe this was what paved the way for the syndicate to use the facilities for the purpose of smuggling.”
Authorities across East and Southeast Asia seized a total of 349 tonnes of methamphetamine in 2025, with Southeast Asia alone accounting for 94 per cent of global seizures of the drug, according to data from the UN Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC).
It was a more than five-fold surge from the 65 tonnes seized in East and Southeast Asia just a decade earlier as drug traffickers quickly shifted their focus to synthetic drugs, which the UNODC said were cheaper to make and transport compared with the cost of maintaining sprawling poppy plantations needed to create heroin and other drugs.
Saifuddin said 1kg of methamphetamine could fetch about 50,000 ringgit in Malaysia, but earnings rose exponentially to about 250,000 ringgit a kilogram in Indonesia and as much as 450,000 ringgit per kilogram on the international market.
“This is a very lucrative business … this is not only a question of serious crime, but it also undermines the integrity of [Malaysia’s] security and defence institutions,” the minister said.
By Joseph Sipalan

title_en: China and Netherlands send ‘positive signal’ over global controls on military AI
content_en:
The Dutch occupy a key niche in the global tech industry and recently unveiled plans to boost their military-industrial hi-tech base.
The Dutch firm ASML has found itself in the cross hairs of a US bid to restrict tech exports to China. Photo: ASML
China and the Netherlands have agreed on the need for international regulations on the military use of AI, a move hailed as an encouraging step forward.
The two countries agreed on the necessity of global cooperation on artificial intelligence and the opportunities and risks from the technology, according to a joint statement issued on Wednesday after Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi met his Dutch counterpart, Tom Berendsen, in Beijing.
The Netherlands plays a key role in the global tech industry and recently unveiled a plan to avoid over-reliance on one source of AI, an approach analysts said Chinese open-source models could help support.
“The two sides support enhancing multilateral governance of military applications of AI and support the United Nations in fulfilling its due role,” the statement read.
The pair also discussed the importance of maintaining close communications and export control dialogue.
[embedded media]
Managing risks in the military domain was particularly urgent as AI was already being integrated into active warfare, said Huang Jing, a professor of international relations at Shanghai International Studies University, citing the US military’s use of the technology during its war on Iran.
Dialogue was essential to keeping the military use of AI from spiralling out of control globally, Huang added, describing the inclusion of this point in the joint statement as “a very positive signal”.
“While Europe may not be a major AI player in terms of frontier development, it is a major AI governance player,” John Gong, a professor of economics at the University of International Business and Economics in Beijing, said.
Developing cutting-edge AI required massive investment in capital, talent and energy – conditions Europe currently lacked, Gong added.
With both Washington and Beijing already discussing AI governance, European countries did not want to be left out, particularly given the Dutch strengths in both technology and defence, he said.
Huang said: “Amid broader turmoil across Europe, the Netherlands stands out as a relatively stable country with strong hi-tech capabilities, including chipmaking equipment giant ASML.”
The country has one of the 10 biggest defence budgets in US dollar terms among European members of Nato, according to data from the alliance.
Earlier this month, the Dutch government unveiled a plan to expand its defence technological and industrial base by 40 per cent by 2030, including targeted investments in unmanned and autonomous systems.
The Dutch government also recently launched a national AI strategy designed to reduce its reliance on both American and Chinese companies.
[embedded media]
“If US closed-source models shut you out, China’s open-source ecosystem remains open,” Huang said. “If the Netherlands can cooperate with China, it can secure a seat at the table. How far that cooperation goes remains to be seen, but it is at least a positive start.”
Gong said: “For European countries, the goal in AI is to avoid being forced to take sides – and China welcomes that approach.”
He said transatlantic relations were undergoing a profound shift, with Europe growing increasingly reluctant to accept unilateral decisions from Washington.
Speaking to reporters in Beijing on Wednesday, Berendsen said export controls were a matter for the Netherlands to decide, citing the US Match (Multilateral Alignment of Technology Controls on Hardware) Act that seeks to further restrict exports of advanced chipmaking equipment to China.
The bipartisan act, which has gained further traction following the scandal over Nvidia chief Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy, would require US allies to adopt stricter export controls or face unilateral restrictions on their equipment, including ASML’s immersion deep ultraviolet lithography tools.
According to Dutch news agency ANP, Berendsen said the act “must not be passed. That is the most important thing.”
ASML’s advanced lithography equipment is critical to producing cutting-edge chips, and the firm expects China to account for roughly 20 per cent of its sales this year, according to Reuters.
Meanwhile, a dispute over Nexperia, a Dutch semiconductor maker acquired by Chinese firm Wingtech Technology in 2019, has intensified sharply over the past year.
After a Dutch court ruling stripped Wingtech of management control, it this month authorised court-appointed administrators to seek outside investors while prohibiting the Chinese parent company from interfering. Wingtech has pledged to contest the ruling.
By Carol Yang

title_en: China’s appetite for Russian farm goods grows despite thaw in US trade ties
content_en:
Russia’s agricultural exports to China are hitting records, but analysts say they cannot replace key US supplies.
An exhibitor arranges a Russian king crab at a China-Russia expo in Harbin, Heilongjiang province. Photo: Xinhua
From vegetable oil to seafood, Russia’s agricultural exports to China are hitting new milestones, even as US and Chinese officials move to stabilise a farm trade relationship increasingly overshadowed by geopolitics.
Three Russian exports – rapeseed oil, crab and frozen pollock – each surpassed US$1 billion in sales to China in the first 10 months of this year, the Federal Centre for Agricultural Export Development under Russia’s Ministry of Agriculture said earlier this week.
The records reflect surging bilateral trade, with Western sanctions over the war in Ukraine pushing Moscow to find new markets, while Beijing seeks to diversify its import sources and cut reliance on any single supplier.
China bought nearly US$8 billion worth of Russian farm produce from January to September, a year-on-year increase of 42 per cent, according to calculations by China’s food and agricultural trade chamber based on customs data.
Overall trade between China and Russia rose by more than 30 per cent in value terms during the first 10 months.
The surge came amid talks between China, the world’s largest net importer of agricultural products, and the United States, one of its major suppliers, to strengthen agricultural trade through mutual tariff cuts and Beijing’s specific purchase commitments, estimated to be worth nearly US$30 billion a year.
The two countries held the first meeting of the Agriculture Working Group under the China-US Trade Council in Beijing on Monday and Tuesday. The two sides had “candid, in-depth and constructive exchanges” on issues including agricultural product regulation and market access, according to an official readout, which provided few further details.
The increase in imports from the northern neighbour is quite considerable, but … not enough to have a major impact on trade with the USZhang Zhixian, Cngrain.com
“The primary factor driving China’s imports of agricultural products from Russia and the US is the growth in China’s demand for agricultural products,” said Song Guoyou, a deputy director of Fudan University’s Centre for American Studies.
“Diversified agricultural imports also contribute to China’s food security,” he said, adding that Russian and American farm shipments largely served different needs and were not direct substitutes for one another.
Russian shipments of soybeans – the top US agricultural export to China – reached US$548 million from January to October, more than double the full-year total for 2025, according to Chinese customs figures.
However, these imports consisted entirely of non-genetically modified varieties, setting them apart from American supplies. They also remain only a fraction of China’s commitment to buy 25 million tonnes of American soybeans annually, a volume worth more than US$10 billion.
Zhang Zhixian, head of research at Henan-based research firm Cngrain.com, said China was a “breakthrough point” for Russia, pointing to both geographic proximity and Moscow’s declining shipments to other destinations due to the Russia-Ukraine conflict.
“The increase in imports from the northern neighbour is quite considerable, but the absolute volume is not large … not enough to have a major impact [on trade with the US],” Zhang said.
Russia has also significantly increased overland trade through rail corridors to China and other countries as traditional maritime routes across the Black Sea and Baltic Sea face disruption.
From July to October, overland grain shipments to China surged sixfold from a year earlier, Russia’s Interfax news agency quoted a senior grain industry official as saying last week.
While European and US sanctions have caused trade with the West to plummet, Russia has largely turned towards China, India and economies across the Middle East and Central Asia.
President Vladimir Putin said the Russian economy was “moving at full speed ahead, even faster than expected” at last week’s Apec CEO Summit.
By Mandy Zuo

title_en: Tai Po fire: remembering the victims
content_en:
The South China Morning Post has created a full-page infographic to remember the 168 people killed in the blaze one year ago.
The South China Morning Post has created an infographic to remember the Tai Po fire victims. Photo: SCMP
Hong Kong is still healing, one year after a devastating inferno engulfed Tai Po’s Wang Fuk Court residential complex. Survivors are trying to move forward while grieving loved ones – parents, spouses, siblings and children – whom they lost without the chance to say goodbye.
The South China Morning Post has created a full-page infographic to remember the 168 people killed in the fire. The petals symbolise the lives lost – people held forever in the hearts of their families, friends and the city.
The infographic remembering the Tai Po fire victims. Photo: SCMP
Click here for a larger version of the infographic or read on for more details.
Generations lost
Thirty-seven households lost more than two family members in the fire. In one case, a grandmother, her son, his one-year-old daughter and a domestic helper died together.
Thirty-seven households lost more than two family members. Photo: SCMP
Firefighter’s sacrifice
Firefighter Ho Wai-ho, 37, died in the line of duty. The independent committee investigating the fire praised him for putting the rescue of others above his own safety in perilous conditions, saying he exemplified the highest standards of selflessness and dedication.
Firefighter Ho Wai-ho died in the line of duty. Photo: SCMP
Domestic helpers who stayed until the end
Among the deceased were 10 domestic helpers – nine Indonesians and one Filipino – who worked on the estate and remained with their employers until the end.
Among the dead were 10 domestic helpers. Photo: SCMP
Women and the elderly
Nearly 70 per cent of the victims – 114 people – were 65 or older, many of whom had called the estate home for decades. Seven were children aged under 18. Women accounted for most of the victims. Of the 168 people who died in the fire, 110 were female and 58 were male.
Nearly 70 per cent of the victims, 114 people, were 65 or older. Photo: SCMP
