title_en: Could EU delisting of Chinese firm pave way for wider sanctions relief?
content_en:
Beijing welcomes lifting of sanctions on home textiles maker and urges further delistings as it reviews relief requests from European firms.
Beijing has received applications from EU companies seeking removal from China’s export-control list, according to the Ministry of Commerce. Photo: Getty Images
After the European Union lifted sanctions on Chinese home textiles maker Yusha Group, Beijing says it hopes the bloc will remove more domestic firms from its blacklist, as it reviews applications from EU companies seeking relief from its own export-control restrictions.
“We welcome the move, which will help create a favourable environment for normal business cooperation between the two sides,” China’s Ministry of Commerce said on Thursday in response to the EU’s decision to remove Yusha from its Russia-related sanctions list.
“We hope the EU will continue to remove more Chinese companies from its sanctions list,” a ministry statement said.
It added that Beijing had recently received written applications from relevant EU companies seeking removal from China’s export-control list and was conducting “delisting review procedures”.
Yusha was among a group of entities blacklisted by the EU in February 2025 over allegations that they had supported Russia’s military-industrial complex in its war against Ukraine.
The move comes after China and the EU agreed in October to launch delisting procedures for companies on their respective export-control lists under their own legal frameworks.
As part of broader trade talks, the two sides also agreed to cap Chinese hybrid car shipments to the bloc over the next four years, while Beijing pledged to continue facilitating export licence approvals for rare earths and permanent magnets destined for the EU.
A new consensus between Washington and Moscow on sanctions could prompt the US to adjust restrictions on Chinese companies accused of Russia-related businessZhao Minghao, Centre for American Studies at Fudan University
On Wednesday, the European Council said in a press release that it had decided to remove one entity from the list subject to tighter export restrictions, without identifying the company.
“The entity has stopped the behaviour that led to its listing and has given credible assurances that it will not trade sensitive goods with Russia,” the council said.
A notice published in the EU’s Official Journal on Thursday identified the delisted entity as Yusha. The decision was due to take effect on Friday, the notice said.
Zhao Minghao, a deputy director of the Centre for American Studies at Fudan University, said the EU’s decision and China’s review of European applications should primarily be seen as a gesture of “mutual goodwill” amid efforts to avoid a trade war.
“Both China and the EU recognise that safeguarding economic and trade relations has become increasingly important,” Zhao said, pointing to recent consultations between the two sides as well as proposed new US tariffs.
It is not the first time the bloc has eased restrictions on a Chinese company. In June, EU ministers paused restrictions on Chinese chipmaker Yangzhou Yangjie Electronic Technology, which had been sanctioned in an earlier round of measures targeting Russia’s war effort.
The South China Morning Post previously reported that diplomats from the EU’s 27 member states came under pressure in October to lift sanctions on Yusha. In return, Beijing pledged that the company would refrain from shipping banned items to Russian military-linked buyers.
Zhao said, however, that the EU’s move was unlikely to have a direct impact on Washington’s approach towards Chinese companies.
“What is truly critical going forward is whether negotiations between the US and Russia lead to an easing of tensions,” he said.
A new consensus between Washington and Moscow on sanctions could prompt the US to adjust restrictions on Chinese companies accused of Russia-related business, Zhao added.
Yusha was placed on the US Commerce Department’s Entity List in August 2024, six months before the EU imposed its own sanctions, over similar allegations linked to Russia.
Beijing has consistently opposed such US measures, describing them as a typical example of unilateral sanctions and “long-arm jurisdiction”.
In August, the US removed the Istanbul branch of Turkish company Atempo from its Entity List after it had been accused of involvement in Russia-related procurement activities.
By Sherry Wang

title_en: PLA overhauls joint training after drills expose coordination gaps
content_en:
Mock friendly fire and airspace clashes prompt Chinese military to rethink how different services train to fight as an integrated force.
A PLA Navy sailor monitors a guided-missile frigate during the “Joint Sword” military exercises around Taiwan on April 10, 2023. Photo: Military Department of China National Radio
China’s military is overhauling how its various services train together as joint exercises continue to expose shortcomings in the People’s Liberation Army’s ability to fight as an integrated force.
In the latest example, a navy destroyer flotilla under the PLA’s Eastern Theatre Command changed how it trains with other services following drills in which airforce jets were twice judged to have been “shot down” by friendly forces.
A PLA Rocket Force unit also struggled to guide strikes against moving targets at sea during the manoeuvres, according to a report by the Chinese military newspaper PLA Daily on Monday.
Under revised training arrangements, the flotilla now shares its training waters and targets with other services and designs joint exercises around their training requirements.
The changes also include regular cross-service personnel exchanges, with one recent exercise plan calling for warships to use information from other services to provide terminal guidance for long-range strikes.
The initiatives reflect Beijing’s push to translate a decade of military reforms and rapid weapons modernisation into joint combat capabilities. Analysts say that overcoming barriers to cross-service integration will be crucial to China’s ability to fully exploit its growing arsenal of advanced warships, aircraft and missiles in a major conflict.
China has long recognised the need to improve coordination between its military services. The rapid defeat of Iraqi forces by a US-led coalition in 1991 demonstrated the effectiveness of combining advanced weapons, information technology and closely coordinated operations across military services. The Gulf War helped spur extensive PLA research into joint operations, with Beijing advocating greater integration from the mid-2000s.
These efforts culminated in a major restructuring of the PLA’s operational command system in 2016, when Beijing replaced seven military regions with five joint theatre commands responsible for directing cross-service operations.
Under the revised structure, services became mainly responsible for developing capabilities, while permanent joint command organisations were established at national and theatre levels to direct operations in peacetime and wartime.
[embedded media]
Developing joint combat capabilities was “equal in importance to introducing new weapons and equipment, developing new doctrine and conducting training”, said Dennis Blasko, a former US military attache in Beijing.
Alongside those structural changes, Beijing has more recently sought to overhaul how its services train together, with the PLA leadership calling in May last year for greater sharing of training facilities and resources to support integrated joint training.
By October, the PLA Daily was reporting growing cross-service cooperation and the shared use of training facilities. In January, the newspaper described how a naval flotilla had been sharing its training waters with airforce and rocket force units since last year.
Monday’s report described how the Eastern Theatre Command flotilla’s initial efforts to share training facilities exposed further problems. In one instance, conflicting airspace requirements forced participating units to make last-minute adjustments, disrupting training for much of the day.
“The problem of de-conflicting airspace and avoiding fratricide (among their own naval, air and missile forces) especially at sea is a new challenge for the PLA,” Blasko said.
The flotilla subsequently incorporated its annual training plan into a higher-level joint training programme, with resources allocated centrally according to individual units’ requirements.
Other services can now request access to the flotilla’s training resources, with a dedicated naval team incorporating their requirements into joint exercise plans, according to the PLA Daily.
The changes also extend to information sharing. In one exercise, an airforce early warning aircraft transmitted target data and threat assessments to a warship via a data link.
In a separate joint exercise, the time between orders being issued and forces deploying was cut by nearly a third, according to PLA Daily.
[embedded media]
Chinese military commentator Song Zhongping said jointly designing exercises and sharing training facilities were essential because future wars could not be won by a single branch of the military alone and would require all branches to work together as a system.
The PLA would therefore pursue additional ways of integrating its combat capabilities, with particular emphasis on developing information technology and intelligent systems, Song added.
Christian Wirth, a researcher at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs, said the PLA had made considerable progress since broader military reforms began in 2015, citing repeated large-scale exercises around Taiwan since 2022.
Even so, cross-service integration still appears to be a work in progress, with a report published last week by the Centre for Strategic and International Studies finding that the PLA’s ability to conduct joint operations remained uneven. The authors found that the PLA appeared better prepared for joint operations that could be extensively planned in advance than for those requiring rapid, decentralised coordination at the tactical level.
Besides training and procedural adjustments, Wirth said that achieving jointness required changes in mindset “of a kind that military leaders gain only from serving in different services, including as commanders with responsibilities for joint operations, from early on in their careers”.
Beijing appears to be aware of that need. In a separate report on Wednesday, the PLA Daily said the National Defence University’s Joint Operations College had recently organised war games involving mixed teams of students from army, navy and airforce command colleges.
The participants had to integrate the operational thinking of different services into a single operational plan. The newspaper said cross-service study visits and on-site instruction had recorded nearly 20,000 attendances this year.
By Gabriel Dominguez

title_en: Hong Kong exports post fastest growth in 70 years on AI-related goods
content_en:
Shipments soar by 65.6 per cent year on year in October although fresh US tariffs have clouded the outlook.
Kwai Chung Container Terminals. Photo:  Nora Tam
Runaway growth in Hong Kong’s exports, driven by demand for artificial intelligence-related electronic goods, continued into October, with shipments soaring by 65.6 per cent year on year, the fastest pace in more than 70 years, although fresh US tariffs have clouded the outlook.
Provisional figures released by the Census and Statistics Department on Thursday showed that the value of exports rose to a record HK$764.5 billion (US$98 billion) last month, while imports grew by 56.2 per cent to HK$783.8 billion, leaving a trade deficit of HK$19.3 billion.
Hong Kong’s export growth was the fastest since the 70.7 per cent increase recorded in April 1956. That monthly figure has never been broken since records began in January 1953.
[embedded media]
A government spokesman said October’s historic high was marked by continued strong growth in exports of AI-related electronic products.
“Exports of other products also picked up. Taking all product types together, exports to most major markets recorded notable increases,” he said.
Despite the record growth, Hong Kong trade faces fresh headwinds from new tariffs that US President Donald Trump imposed on 14 major economies including China just a week after meeting President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen on the sidelines of an Apec summit.
The new levies, subject to a public comment period, would lift total duties on targeted economies from 15 to 20 per cent. The move comes as the transactional American president looks for alternatives after the US Supreme Court struck down his broad-based “emergency” tariffs in February.
The government spokesman said, looking ahead, robust global AI investment and related demand would continue to support Hong Kong’s merchandise trade performance.
But he warned external uncertainties would persist.
“Developments in international trade and technology policies, risks associated with the rapid expansion of global AI investment, and evolving geopolitical tensions warrant close monitoring,” he said.
Total exports to Asia surged 66.1 per cent in October, with increased outbound trade to most major destinations, led by Taiwan, with a 198.3 per cent rise, and Singapore at 98.9 per cent.
In the first 10 months of 2026, total exports rose by 47.4 per cent year on year, with imports up by 46.2 per cent, resulting in a deficit of HK$438.5 billion.
By Cannix Yau

title_en: Shanghai party chief’s downfall shows reach of anti-corruption drive
content_en:
Chen Jining is the fourth Politburo member since 2022 to be targeted in push to stamp out corruption ahead of leadership reshuffle.
Chen Jining (above, centre) is the fourth member of China’s decision-making Politburo appointed in 2022 to fall from grace. Photo: Reuters
Shanghai’s Communist Party chief, Chen Jining, was placed under investigation for corruption as China’s widening anti-corruption drive toppled a fourth Politburo member ahead of a major leadership reshuffle next year.
Chen is suspected of “serious breaches of discipline and law”, state broadcaster CCTV reported on Tuesday, using a common euphemism for corruption. The Central Commission for Discipline Inspection (CCDI) and the National Commission of Supervision are investigating the case.
The downfall of Chen, 62, removes a rising political star who hosted international political and business leaders in Shanghai, spearheaded national artificial intelligence initiatives and had been seen as a possible candidate to succeed President Xi Jinping. The 73-year-old Xi also previously served as party chief in China’s financial capital, as did former president Jiang Zemin and Premier Li Qiang.
Chen’s detention underlines an acceleration in the anti-corruption drive ahead of next year’s 21st National Congress, where Xi will probably secure a fourth term in office. The country’s top anti-corruption watchdog has detained 61 high-ranking officials so far this year, closing in on 2025’s record full-year tally of 65 “tigers” (see SCMP Plus Quick Digest). Anti-corruption has been a key focus since Xi took power in 2012.
The Politburo now has just 21 active members, the fewest since 1999. Ma Xingrui and former military leaders He Weidong and Zhang Youxia have also been ousted from the original 24 members chosen in 2022. General Zhang Shengmin joined the body last month.
[embedded media]
Related news:
Shanghai’s senior Communist Party leaders pledged “to maintain absolute loyalty to the party, to oppose corruption with a clear stance and to stay in high-level alignment with the Central Committee” following the announcement of the Chen investigation. The city’s official Jiefeng Daily newspaper reported on its front page that the leadership had a late-night meeting to discuss the case. They determined that it demonstrated the Central Committee’s resolve “to persistently advance comprehensive and strict party governance”, according to Reuters.
Liu Min, a senior official at the Ministry of Science and Technology, has been placed under investigation for corruption, China’s top anti-corruption watchdog said on Monday. She will face a disciplinary review by the ministry’s CCDI team. Xie Jun, a deputy general manager at state energy giant China National Petroleum Corp., is also “undergoing disciplinary review and supervisory investigation”, the CCDI said on Sunday. A former general manager of state-owned China National Nuclear Corp., Gu Jun, was charged with bribery by the Supreme People’s Procuratorate last week.
A Chinese ministry official was sentenced to death after leaking more than 100 state secrets to a foreign intelligence agency, according to a rare disclosure on Monday from the state security apparatus. The official, only identified as Ma, was stripped of political rights and had all personal property confiscated, said Baomiguan, a social-media channel tied to the National Administration of State Secrets Protection. The ministry and the foreign intelligence agency weren’t identified. There was also no mention of whether the sentence had been carried out.
How others reported it
Access risk: The takedown of Chen is particularly significant given his high profile and his deep involvement in critical policy areas such as AI, climate and education. For companies and investors, the purge exposes the fragility of strategies built around access to individual leaders. Businesses can lose influential advocates overnight, while relationships once considered assets can become causes of scrutiny. (Bloomberg Economics)
Reality check: David Zhang, an analyst at Trivium China, suggested that the latest investigation should be read in the context of last month’s fifth plenum. “Xi, again, stressed party discipline as a long-term undertaking,” Zhang said. “He means business, and doesn’t see party discipline as a distraction from addressing economic challenges. For anyone who thinks broader economic pressures will make Beijing ease off on political controls, this is a clear reality check.” (Nikkei Asia)
No warning signs: “Chen’s purge is particularly shocking in that he poses no military threat, and doesn’t deviate from Xi on major symbolic issues like ethnic policy,” [Wen-Ti Sung, a non-resident fellow at the Atlantic Council’s Global China Hub,] said, referring to Xi’s emphasis on integration into mainstream Chinese culture. “But he got purged anyway, so far without even an explanation. The shock is bound to reverberate.” (Reuters)
AI expertise: Chen Jining, Party Secretary of Shanghai and CCP rising star, has been detained for corruption. Former Tsinghua [University] president and Beijing mayor. Very big deal for China’s AI ecosystem. Of all top leaders, he was most in touch with the key players across frontier companies, labs etc. (Matt Sheehan, fellow of the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, on X.com)
Who’s next?: “Who on this Politburo feels safe, especially as the personnel machinations for next year’s Party Congress intensify?” China analyst Bill Bishop wrote in his Sinocism newsletter. Chen’s investigation came as a surprise, according to Bishop, given rumours were swirling that another senior official, not Chen, would fall next in the anti-corruption campaign. (BBC)
The SCMP Plus takeaway
The pathway from Shanghai to the top echelons of China’s Communist Party was so well worn in the late 1990s that a political adage did the rounds: Let the comrades from Shanghai board first.
Chen Jining seemed next in line to ride the train, with widespread speculation that he would be promoted into the party’s highest decision-making body, the Politburo Standing Committee, at a five-yearly Party Congress next autumn.
Then came this week’s shock announcement that the Shanghai party chief had become the latest target of a relentless nationwide anti-corruption drive.
Chen was elevated to Shanghai general secretary, and into the 24-member Politburo, in 2022 after serving as Beijing mayor for five years. As head of China’s commercial and financial capital, and a fluent English speaker, he hosted visiting foreign business leaders including Elon Musk, who has a Tesla gigafactory in the city, and Apple executive chairman Tim Cook. He presided over the World Artificial Intelligence Conference in July.
Promotion to the standing committee appeared almost guaranteed. Eight of the nine Shanghai party bosses before Chen made the leap, starting with Jiang Zemin, who became national party general secretary under paramount leader Deng Xiaoping in 1989.
Shanghai is a traditional proving ground for top leadership because of the city’s critical importance to China’s economy, social development and politics.
Other veterans of the city’s top job include former premier Zhu Rongji, as well as Wu Bangguo and Huang Ju, Jiang allies who joined the standing committee at the 16th Party Congress in 2002.
President Xi Jinping, who was briefly Shanghai party chief in 2007, joined the Standing Committee at the 17th Party Congress the same year. Chen’s predecessor Li Qiang is now China’s premier.
The only exception to the rule was Chen Liangyu, who was ousted in 2006 in relation to the misuse of Shanghai’s social security funds in the city’s biggest corruption scandal.
Chen Jining’s ousting this week stands out in comparison because it appeared to come out of the blue. Rumours circulated well ahead of Chen Liangyu’s downfall two decades ago. There was similar gossip about Xinjiang party chief and Politburo member Ma Xingrui, who was dismissed from office and stripped of party membership earlier this year.
The shock felling of a Shanghai party chief underlines that no one can be considered safe at the top.
Four Politburo members – including Chen – have now fallen since Xi began his latest five-year term in 2022. That is unprecedented since the Gang of Four – all Politburo members – were arrested after Mao Zedong’s death in 1976. They were all expelled the following year under then party chief Hua Guofeng.
Three retired Politburo members were also purged during Xi’s previous terms.
Chen’s ousting sends a strong message ahead of a personnel reshuffle at next year’s party congress that Xi’s overriding priority is party discipline. Party members undergo rigorous screening ahead of the congress, including reviews of their performance, reputation, personal connections and political resources. Now, anti-corruption credentials will be a key criterion for promotion. Failure to pass will signal no future advancement, and the likelihood of being targeted by anti-corruption and party discipline agencies.
Xi has long seen corruption as the biggest threat to the party’s rule and China’s rise, arguing that the Communist Party is the only institution capable of organising, mobilising and deploying the nation’s social resources.
“China’s success hinges on the party,” he said in a 2021 speech marking the party’s centenary. “Any attempt to divide the party from the Chinese people is bound to fail.”
The party’s 100 million members operate under uniquely tight and strict discipline – there are no other checks or balances in place.
The concern is that a lack of discipline will lead to the party’s deterioration or even collapse, destabilising society and threatening China’s development. In short, to the leadership, fighting corruption is a matter of survival – an end in itself, not a means to achieving something else.
Chen’s age is also noteworthy. At 62, he was among the youngest members of the Politburo, and thus a target of speculation about promotion and succession planning. His ousting removes an up-and-comer from the scene, and perhaps makes it more likely that older members of the standing committee will get another term next year.
Xi will eventually need to promote the next generation of leaders, but the ongoing corruption campaign signals that he wants to ensure that candidates are squeaky clean before they move up the ladder – avoiding the trouble of having to clean house after the reshuffle.
By Brian Rhoads, Raymond Ma

title_en: Nepal starts legal process to declare 4,000 dead 3 months after fatal floods
content_en:
A change in Nepal’s laws last month reduced the waiting period to declare disaster victims dead from 12 years to around six weeks.
A torrent of muddy water surges past houses and through the Trishuli river in the aftermath of flash floods, at Betrawati in Nepal’s Nuwakot district on August 29. Photo: AFP)
Nepal had begun a process to legally declare dead thousands of people still missing after its catastrophic summer floods, authorities said on Thursday, three months after the disaster.
A high-altitude glacier on the Nepal-China border collapsed on August 26, unleashing a torrent of water, ice, rock and debris. In Nepal, the floods killed more than 1,400 people and left over 5,500 missing.
“We have started the process to declare the missing dead by verifying their details,” said Ram Bahadur KC, spokesman for the disaster management authority.
Authorities have issued public notices naming about 4,000 missing people, including 623 foreign nationals, and asked for objections or corrections before formal declarations are made.
[embedded media]
Additional names can be added following further verification, with the government expected to issue death declarations once legal procedures are completed.
The move follows a change in Nepal’s laws last month, reducing the waiting period to declare disaster victims dead from 12 years to around six weeks.
The flood was one of the deadliest disasters in the Himalayan nation’s history.
Despite weeks of rescue operations involving hundreds of workers combing through mountains of mud and debris, only a handful of missing people were found alive. Just 112 bodies have so far been identified and returned to their families.
Relatives mourn during symbolic funerals held for flood victims still reported missing at Pashupatinath temple in Kathmandu on September 2. Photo: AFP
The absence of death certificates has left many families unable to claim compensation, transfer property or settle other legal matters. Some families have already held symbolic cremation ceremonies for those whose bodies have never been recovered.
In China, state media reported in September that 43 people had died and 519 were missing on the Tibetan side of the border, saying the situation was “still under further investigation”.
Beijing has not provided an update since then, and when asked on Thursday, a Chinese foreign ministry spokesman directed the question to the “competent authorities”.
By Agence France-Presse

title_en: What others can learn from China’s effective governance
content_en:
The Communist Party’s commitment to self-supervision and self-governance offers valuable inspiration for political parties around the world.
President Xi Jinping, general secretary of the Communist Party of China Central Committee, delivers an address at the fifth plenary session of the 20th CPC Central Committee in Beijing on October 29. Photo: Xinhua
To understand China today, one must understand the Communist Party of China. The close attention the world paid to the fifth plenum of the 20th party congress, held in Beijing last month, underscores the global significance and contemporary relevance of this century-old party’s experience in self-supervision and self-governance.
These are strands of historical DNA running through the entire course of the party. The plenary session noted that the party has achieved one victory after another because it has attached great importance to self-supervision and self-governance while having the courage to uphold truth and correct errors, growing stronger by relying on its efforts and the support of the people to resolve its own problems.
It advanced party building during periods of revolution, development and reform and had made further progress since the 18th national congress in 2012.
During this time, the party found two answers to the question of how to escape the historical cycle of rise and fall: people’s oversight of the government and the party’s self-reform. These are unique discoveries by the Communist Party of China, and they will forever stand out in the history of Marxist parties.
Rigorous supervision and governance of the party are vital safeguards for China’s high-quality development. Governance of the country must begin with governance of the party, and governance of the party must be undertaken rigorously. Only a strong party can make a strong China.
The plenary session spoke highly of the historic achievements made in rigorous party self-governance in the new era. It was agreed that the Central Committee, with President Xi Jinping at its core, has shown tremendous political courage and a strong sense of responsibility, staying committed to party self-governance by introducing stringent measures and making continuous efforts to tackle prominent issues.
[embedded media]

title_en: Reopened China-Mongolia-Russia railway expected to boost cross-border trade and tourism
content_en:
Trains stopped in February 2020 on the longer Beijing-Moscow route, which began in 1959, amid travel restrictions to control the spread of Covid-19.
The China-Mongolia-Russia international passenger train departs from Beijing Railway Station  on Wednesday. Photo: Xinhua
After a six-year hiatus, a direct China-Mongolia-Russia passenger railway service reopened this week in a move expected to boost trade and tourism among the three countries.
The first international passenger train to traverse the 2,666km (1,657-mile) route since 2020 left from Beijing Railway Station on Wednesday. Round trips would be offered on a weekly basis, according to China State Railway Group.
Trips between Beijing and the eastern Siberian industrial city Irkutsk, which is at the end of the newly opened passenger line, take about 55 hours. Trains stop in the Mongolian capital Ulaanbaatar, among other cities.
The service that reopened this week covers part of the longer Beijing-Moscow route, which dates back to 1959 and had stopped operating in February 2020 as governments restricted travel to control the spread of Covid-19. Passengers heading for Moscow can transfer to another train in Russia.
The carriages, which are made in China, include a dining car and sleeping compartments.
Xinhua said the railway service would promote “economic and trade cooperation” along with “people-to-people exchanges” among the three countries.
Passengers board the China-Mongolia-Russia international passenger train at the Beijing Railway Station on Wednesday. Photo: Xinhua
“The main benefit is that it makes it easier for people who do business across the border to meet,” said Xu Tianchen, a senior China economist with The Economist Intelligence Unit in Beijing.
Traders and small businesses may use the trains as “another way” to visit suppliers, meet distributors and check shipments, Xu said. Hotels, restaurants and tour operators along the route would earn business from train travellers, he added.
Tourists today can ride in a direct sleeper car from Beijing through Mongolia to the scenic Lake Baikal region of Russia, Xu said. “Tour operators can build three-country itineraries around it, and for some travellers the journey itself is part of the attraction.”
The Beijing-Moscow trains are also known for a string of armed bandit attacks in 1993 that hit Chinese merchants who were using the railway to take goods to resource-scarce, post-Soviet Russia and carry cash back home. Chinese police cracked down that year on rapes, assaults and robberies.
“The current restart is not simply a return to the old status quo, but a test of whether the infrastructure and passenger demand have endured,” Russia-based news outlet Pravda.ru said on Thursday.
“For those seeking an alternative to aviation, the train offers a different kind of engagement with Asia,” it added.

title_en: Chinese group to develop 10 smart city sites in Indonesia under US$50 billion deal
content_en:
Country’s sovereign wealth fund makes deal with a Shaanxi Construction-led consortium for ‘future smart city’ sites in undisclosed locations.
Indonesia intends to build smart cities to ease congestion and pollution in existing urban areas. Photo: VCG via Getty Images
A Chinese consortium has reached an initial agreement with Indonesia’s sovereign wealth fund to develop 10 smart city sites in the Southeast Asian country, part of a package of two-way deals, the Indonesian side said.
An entity under the fund Danantara signed the US$50 billion memorandum of understanding to develop smart cities across the archipelago of 288 million people. The Chinese consortium would develop about 1.5 million housing units and supporting infrastructure for roughly 3 million people in each city, the Indonesian government said.
The deal would be the largest in a suite of investments and commitments arranged by the two countries at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) leaders’ meeting in Shenzhen last week.
On its website, Indonesia’s Cabinet Secretariat described the project as “initial ‘future smart city’ sites”, without detailing their locations or scales. Shaanxi Construction Engineering Group would lead the consortium, the secretariat said.
Indonesia intends to build smart cities – those that use networked sensors and cameras to process data that improves efficiency or quality of life – to ease congestion and pollution in existing urban areas.
Indonesia and China signed a series of agreements at the Apec summit. Photo: Handout
China already had about 500 pilot smart-city projects in progress as of 2018, representing more than half of the world’s total, the official Xinhua News Agency said.
Equipped with the experience of developing those cities at home, Chinese developers want to expand their businesses overseas, according to a 2021 brief published by the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology.
Indonesia was probably “eager to jump” on the deal to ensure it would receive some of the Chinese investments being made worldwide, said James Chin, a professor of Asian studies at the University of Tasmania in Australia.
“They do need smart cities,” Chin said. “Indonesia is really lacking in key infrastructure.”
Chinese contractors had the experience, pricing and fast work timetables that Indonesia would want, said Paramitaningrum, an international relations lecturer at Bina Nusantara University in Jakarta.
Other China-Indonesia agreements reached at Apec covered manufacturing and technology, infrastructure financing and the development of coal-to-ethanol technology, the Cabinet Secretariat said.
